stories.headline: Karnataka High Court strikes down law to increase reservation for SCs/STs, declares it unconstitutional
stories.deck: Court says 50% ceiling on total reservation is binding constitutional principle
stories.bodyText:
In a major blow to the State government, the High Court of Karnataka on Monday struck down the law to increase reservation for Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs) beyond the 50% ceiling, holding that the enhancement was “constitutionally impermissible.”
A Division Bench comprising Chief Justice Vibhu Bakhru and Justice K.S. Hemalekha declared Sections 3 and 4 of the Karnataka Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Reservation of Seats in Educational Institutions and of Appointments or Posts in the Services under the State) Act, 2022 ultra vires the Constitution and struck down these two provisions.
During Bommai regime
The Act, which came into force retrospectively from November 1, 2022, during the previous BJP government under Basavaraj Bommai, had increased reservation for SCs from 15% to 17% and for STs from 3% to 7%. Since the 32% reservation for Other Backward Classes (OBCs) remained unchanged, the aggregate reservation in the State rose from 50% to 56%, breaching the judicially established 50% ceiling laid down by the Supreme Court in the 1992 case of Indra Sawhney vs Union of India (1992) and subsequently reaffirmed in numerous decisions.
The Bench delivered its verdict on a batch of petitions, including a public interest litigation filed by social worker Mahendra Kumar Mitra and a petition by civil engineering graduates Sagar H.R and others, who had challenged the reservation in recruitment to the Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike (BBMP) based on increased reservation quota.
The 50% principle
The main focus of the Bench’s judgment was on the question of whether the State could exceed the 50% limit for reservation. The Bench, in its 170-page judgment, extensively relying on the apex court’s findings on ceiling for reservations, concluded that the 50% limit is not a mere rule of prudence but a binding constitutional principle that embodies the balance between equality of opportunity and affirmative action.
“The ceiling limit of 50% has to be understood as circumscribing the power of the State to provide for reservation within the said parameters, notwithstanding the numerical strength of the backward classes,” the Bench observed.
State’s argument
The Bench rejected the State’s argument that the 103rd Constitutional Amendment, which introduced 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS), had obliterated the 50% rule. The Bench clarified that the EWS quota is carved out from the general merit pool and does not permit the State to expand reservation for backward classes beyond the ceiling.

stories.headline: Rahul Gandhi’s plea not listed for hearing on October 13, faces routine clerical hurdles
stories.deck: Under the Supreme Court Rules, when a petition has defects, the petitioner is typically given a time window, such as 28 days or standard registry timelines, depending on the specific filing chapter to cure the defects
stories.bodyText:
A petition filed by Opposition leaders led by Rahul Gandhi in the Supreme Court for a complete disclosure of records and decisions of the Election Commission of India (ECI) on the Special Intensive Revision and an independent probe into allegations of unilateral exercise of power by Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, which led to voter deletions and modifications, is not listed for hearing on October 13.
The petition was filed on Monday (October 12, 2026) evening even as Mr. Gandhi led a march to the Supreme Court.
He and the other leaders across the Opposition political spectrum had come to the Supreme Court Registry to mark their presence as petitioners in the case.
The petition points out that it was filed pursuant to a written communication from the CJI on October 11 in response to a representation on behalf of Mr. Gandhi, who is the Leader of Opposition, and co-petitioner, Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge, on October 10 for permission to meet the top judge.
In his response to the Congress leaders’ representation, the CJI informed the two Opposition leaders that “incidentally, some matters highlighting similar issues are scheduled for hearing on Tuesday [October 13, 2026]”. These pending petitions are listed before a three-judge Bench headed by Chief Justice Kant himself.
The CJI had advised the Opposition leaders that they too could file a petition on October 12 between 10.30 a.m. and 4.30 p.m. or use the e-filing facility afforded by the apex court to litigants.
“You have my assurance that any such petition shall be heard at the earliest possible opportunity, in accordance with law,” Chief Justice Kant had written to the Opposition leaders in his October 11 reply.
But the petition is still with the Supreme Court Registry due to routine clerical defects.
Under the Supreme Court Rules, when a petition or appeal has defects or is returned by the Registry, the petitioner or advocate is typically given a time window, such as 28 days or standard registry timelines depending on the specific filing chapter to cure the defects.
If defects are not cured within the initial timeframe and the matter remains in default for up to 90 days, a ‘condonation of defects and refiling’ application can be filed by the petitioners. The matter is routinely placed before a Judge-in-Chambers for orders. The Chamber Judge frequently grants a final extension of time, typically four to six weeks, to clear the objections.
If the defects are still not cured despite opportunities, matters are sometimes listed for dismissal or dismissed for non-prosecution/non-removal of defects. Petitioners routinely file applications for restoration, and the Supreme Court Registry generally adopts a lenient approach in restoring, provided sufficient cause or compliance is shown.
Once the petition is cured, it is numbered, and the Chief Justice of India, as master of the roster, on the administrative side, allots it to an appropriate Bench for preliminary hearing.
Mr. Gandhi’s petition reportedly features over 10 clerical defects, including a deficit in court fees and missing vakalatnamas for some of the petitioners. His legal team said these defects are “contemplated under the Supreme Court Rules and would be cured in due course”. They said the Registry has found no other faults in the substantive legal and constitutional arguments raised in the petition.
Meanwhile, a Bench headed by the Chief Justice is hearing another petition filed by Mr. Gandhi against an Allahabad High Court order, directing the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) and the Directorate of Enforcement (ED) to inquire into the allegations of disproportionate assets made by the private complainant, S. Vignesh Shishir.
The Congress leader had submitted in court that Mr. Shishir’s allegations amounted to a “witch-hunt” and the High Court had passed the order without even affording him a hearing. The apex court had previously halted the disproportionate assets proceedings while orally observing that courts must follow the principles of natural justice.

stories.headline: ‘He is watching from above’: Lalremsiami’s emotional tribute to her late father
stories.deck: Lalremsiami Hmarzote made history by clinching gold at the Asian Games in women's hockey, a pivotal accomplishment for her and her team. She scored vital goals, particularly in the final against China. Remembering her late father, who was her source of motivation, Hmarzote is now determined to inspire young girls in Mizoram to take up hockey and chase their sporting dreams as the Indian women's…
stories.bodyText:
KOLKATA: Lalremsiami Hmarzote’s thoughts drifted to her late father as thousands lined the streets of Mizoram to celebrate India’s historic women’s hockey gold medal at the Asian Games.
“I know he would be proud of me and is watching me from heaven,” the forward told TOI, reflecting on a campaign that saw her score seven goals, including the lone strike in the final against China, as India ended a 44-year wait for Asian Games gold and sealed qualification for the Los Angeles Olympics.
The reception back home was overwhelming for the Mizo star, who returned to a heroine’s welcome after playing a key role in India’s triumphant run.
“The whole of Mizoram celebrated with us. The chief minister, sports minister and so many people came out to welcome us. When we arrived at the airport, there was a grand reception and everyone made us feel very special,” Lalremsiami said.
The roadshow through her hometown of Kolasib, 85km north of the state capital, Aizawl, lined with cheering crowds and children eager to catch a glimpse of their sporting hero, left a deep impression on her. 
“Many children and young people came up to meet me and told me they were inspired by what we had achieved. That made me very happy because if our success can motivate someone to take up sports, then it means a lot,” she said.
While the celebrations were memorable, the Asian Games final remains the defining moment of her career, which began with her India debut in 2017. The occasion carried added significance as it was her 200th international match, and she admitted the pressure before the game was unlike anything she had experienced.
“I was extremely nervous. It was my 200th match, it was the final, and we knew that if we won, we would make history after 44 years and qualify for the LA Olympics,” she said.
“I prayed before the match and asked God to help me. Once the game started, I was able to play freely. To score the goal and help my team and my country win the gold medal was simply amazing. It is a moment I will never forget.”
While many people have supported her journey, much of her motivation, she says, came from her father, who backed her hockey dreams from the very beginning before passing away in 2019.
“My father played a very important role in my career and in my life. He was the one who inspired me and supported me when I was young and just starting hockey. He always believed in me and stood by me every step of the way,” she said. “He is not with us anymore, but the things he told me are still alive inside me. I know he would be proud of me today.”
Lalremsiami also credited the team’s unity, coach Sjoerd Marijne and the support staff for a remarkable run this year that included World Cup qualification, Nations Cup success, a fifth-place finish at the World Cup and Asian Games gold.
“We have gone through a lot of struggles over the years. Our unity within the group has been one of our biggest strengths. Success is not just about the players on the field. It is about the whole team working together,” she said.
The 26-year-old was also part of the Indian side that registered the country’s best Women’s World Cup finish in 52 years. But the focus has already shifted to the Los Angeles Olympics, now less than two years away, and the forward believes India must continue to improve despite becoming Asian champions.
“We have one dream now. We want to do well at the World Cup and win an Olympic medal. We know it will be very challenging, but we are ready for it,” she said.
Even as she dreams of an Olympic podium finish, Lalremsiami hopes to see more girls from Mizoram take up the sport that has given her everything. While the challenges remain, she urged youngsters not to let those limitations hold them back.
“My message to young girls is simple: keep dreaming and keep believing in yourselves. There is a lot of talent in Mizoram. I hope we get more grounds, more academies and better facilities in the future so that more children get the opportunity to play hockey and follow their dreams.”

briefs.headline: France braces for fresh nationwide student demonstrations
briefs.deck: The mobilisation, backed by unions and the far-left Opposition France Unbowed party, was to include a march through Paris starting at 1200 GMT, along with marches in other cities
briefs.bodyText:
France readied on Tuesday (October 13, 2026) for fresh nationwide demonstrations supporting students who have been protesting poor classroom conditions for weeks, with authorities and participants wary of further violence.
The mobilisation, backed by unions and the far-left Opposition France Unbowed party, was to include a march through Paris starting at 1200 GMT, along with marches in other cities.
It follows demonstrations on Thursday (October 8, 2026) that saw more than 70,000 people take to the streets across France, with about 500 people arrested.
French authorities had been hoping that the student protest movement that started in late September was starting to ease, ahead of half-term holidays. The protests have seen students pile up dumpsters and other obstacles to block access to high schools, with clashes occasionally breaking out with police.
On Monday (October 12, 2026), only 130 of France’s 3,700 lycees were closed, according to the education ministry, though it stated that, while “the number of school closures is falling... the violence is intensifying”.
In an incident seemingly unrelated to the protests, police arrested a 14-year-old on Monday near Marseille after a middle school headmaster and a teacher were shot with a hunting rifle, wounding both.
The education ministry said eight members of teaching staff were injured on Monday (October 12, 2026), mostly in the Paris region and cities of Bordeaux and Lyon, in relation to the protests. Its tally did not include the shooting, which police were treating as a separate case.
‘Aren’t being heard’
While most of the protests have been peaceful, students say they are determined to press the government to address the problems of too many absent teachers, dilapidated buildings, overcrowded class schedules and other grievances.
“Students aren’t being heard enough... not their proposals to authorities and elected officials,” a 19-year-old graphic design student in Paris, Leo, said.
He added that the protesters — many of whom were minors — were “disturbed by the level of repression never before seen for a student movement”.
One young protester lost a hand from a police stun grenade earlier in the protests, another lost many of his teeth from a tear-gas canister fired in his face at close range, and another lost an eye.
Rights groups and students have accused the police of a disproportionate use of force.
Several police officers and teachers have also been hurt, and on Monday authorities said fireworks fired through a tube injured two school workers in Reims, one school worker in a Paris suburb and a police officer outside a school in Marseille.
Tuesday’s demonstrations supporting the students were to be followed on Saturday by wider public rallies against the rising cost of living.
Naila, a 17-year-old student in the city of Rennes who said she would participate in Tuesday’s demonstration, hoped it would “converge” with the wider one on Saturday.
President Emmanuel Macron, speaking to reporters on Monday, said the pupils’ grievances would take time to address and urged restraint from protesters.
“These are issues that deserve time, consultations, discussion and respect,” Macron said.
Worries about lost lessons
More than 6,800 people — largely minors — have been taken into police custody over the course of the protests, according to the justice ministry.
Police have opened internal investigations into 24 allegations of brutality against demonstrators.
After last week’s nationwide demonstrations, the government promised some 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed in the coming days to replace absent staff at the 114 worst-affected high schools.
A government spokeswoman on Monday said they had started to be assigned.
But the national students’ union has dismissed the government’s move as “crumbs” and was demanding a 10 billion-euro ($11 billion) boost for lycees.
Some parents and students, however, voiced concerns about all the classes being missed because of the protests. A few worried that the children were being used as pawns by opposition political parties.
Some parents pleaded for the teens to lift their blockades at Paris schools.
“The blockades are by their very nature undemocratic,” complained one mother, who went by the pseudonym Gladys.
“It’s shameful to block students who really want to study, by a movement they aren’t part of,” said Clara Juillet, a university student in the city of Tours who has been unable to attend lessons for a week because of the protests.

briefs.headline: New Zealand-based stepsons shoot UP trader dead over mother’s 2nd marriage; CCTV emerges
briefs.deck: Navjot Singh, a 30-year-old trader, was shot dead inside his shop in Kumhariya Tah village on Saturday. CCTV footage captured two masked men arriving in a silver Maruti Alto before the attack. His father believes his stepsons conspired to kill him due to personal disputes over their mother's marriage. The police are currently searching for the two absconding suspects involved in the murder.
briefs.bodyText:
MEERUT: CCTV footage shows two masked men arriving in a silver Maruti Alto and opening fire at a 30-year-old trader inside his shop in Uttar Pradesh’s Kumhariya Tah village on Saturday evening.
The trader, Navjot Singh, was shot dead around 5pm after he tried to overpower one of the attackers.
The incident took place in the area under Milak Khanam police station.
His father Nishan Singh, a farmer, alleged that Navjot's two stepsons, who live in New Zealand, conspired with a cousin to kill him over their mother's second marriage.
Navjot’s father, Nishan Singh, named seven people in his complaint, including his stepsons, Avdeep and his brother and their cousin Rajandeep. He alleged that they had conspired to murder Navjot.
Stepsons opposed mother’s marriage, says father
According to Nishan, the New Zealand-based stepsons opposed their mother Kamal Kaur’s love marriage to Navjot, which took place a year ago.
Avdeep had returned to India five days before the murder, Nishan said. The father also sought protection for his daughter-in-law following the killing.
Two accused absconding, police say
Additional SP Anurag Singh said Avdeep and Rajandeep, both of whom are absconding, had committed the murder. Police are searching for the two men. The investigation is under way.

briefs.headline: Hackers heat French supermarket fridges, sparking fires and spoiling food
briefs.deck: The Paris prosecutor’s office said that a “large-scale” attack was “affecting connected refrigerators in several ⁠major food retailers across France”, leading to food losses and fires
briefs.bodyText:
Hackers raised the temperature of refrigerators and freezers at hundreds of French supermarkets to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) overnight, causing fires and spoiling food.
The Paris prosecutor’s office said on Monday (October 12, 2026) that a “large-scale” attack was “affecting connected refrigerators in several major food retailers across France”, leading to food losses and fires.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has instructed France’s National Cybersecurity Agency (ANSSI) to investigate, a person in his office said.
France was coordinating with European counterparts because other countries could also be affected, the person said, adding that authorities were assessing whether other French companies were at risk.
Felix Aime, a senior cyber threat intelligence analyst at Sekoia Threat Detection and Research, said Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium had also been affected.
Carrefour said 80 of its supermarkets were hit, while Monoprix, which operates about 490 stores in France, said 5% of its stores were affected.
Les Mousquetaires, owner of retailer Intermarche, said fridges at around 150 of its stores were heated up to 50 C for six hours overnight. A spokesperson said all affected food had been discarded to eliminate health risks.
Paris resident Geert de Clercq witnessed staff at an Intermarche in central Paris throwing cartfuls of defrosted frozen foods into a giant trash container, with molten ice cream sloshing out of broken tubs on the street.
Cooperative U CEO Dominique Schelcher said his supermarket group had also been targeted.
“Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented,” he wrote on X.
Food retailers E.Leclerc and Auchan did not respond to requests for comment.
There was no immediate estimate of industry-wide losses, but Intermarche CEO Thierry Cotillard told BFM TV the “unprecedented” attack would represent losses amounting to “tens of millions of euros nationwide in a single day.”
Christel Delberghe, director general at European retail association Eurocommerce, said, “This incident underlines the importance of resilience across the entire supply chain.”
Cold aisles controllled over internet
Supermarket cold aisles are typically run by control panels that manage an entire store’s fridges and freezers and can be accessed over the internet, which lets maintenance companies adjust them from anywhere.
The source close to Lecornu said ANSSI had identified a vulnerability in software supplied by Danish company Danfoss.
Danfoss said it was “aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems”.
The affected units “were running outdated firmware”, Danfoss said, adding that it had “long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions”.
On August 9, cybersecurity firm Claroty’s Team82 published research detailing vulnerabilities in the Danfoss AK-SM 800A controller. According to the report, software updates issued by Danfoss addressed issues that could have allowed attackers to bypass authentication controls and execute code on compromised devices.
The attacks resemble disruptions reported at about a dozen US military commissaries in late August that led to food losses after fridges were affected.
In a statement, French retail association Fédération du Commerce et de la Distribution called for “full transparency” from Danfoss about the incident. It said supermarkets aimed to protect consumers and return to normal operations as soon as possible. The FCD said some impacted stores were already back up and running.
Dutch security issue
Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, which operates the Netherlands’ largest supermarket chain Albert Heijn and has major operations in the US, said it was dealing with a “security issue” on its network and had taken several systems offline as a precaution.
A message on the retailer’s smartphone app said it was unable to deliver groceries because of a “cybersecurity incident”.
Online orders account for about 10% of Albert Heijn sales. Physical stores remained open, while Dutch news agency ANP reported that rival retailers had seen a surge in delivery orders.
Ahold Delhaize said there was no reason to see a link between the incidents in France and its supermarkets.
Ahold is the fourth-largest grocery retailer in the US. Websites for its Stop & Shop, Giant, Hannaford and Food Lion chains displayed notices saying “site temporarily down”.
It was unclear whether other operations had been affected.

briefs.headline: J&K Waqf Board pushes for uniform Friday sermons, ‘preachers’ committee to decide topics in advance’
briefs.bodyText:
The J&K Waqf Board has pushed for uniform Friday sermons at all mosques in the Union Territory (UT) and will become the first region in the country to adopt this mechanism to ensure the topics to be highlighted at religious places are pre-decided and approved by a committee of preachers.
“Almost a month ago, a directive was issued to all the preachers to have a common khutba (sermon) at all places (of worship). One topic will be selected and the same topic will be highlighted (in the mosques),” Ishtiyaq Mohi-ud-Din, an Executive Magistrate at the Board, told hundreds of preachers who attended the Waqf meeting in a virtual mode from different districts of J&K on Sunday.
He asked the religious leaders to also suggest ways to bring non-Waqf-affiliated mosques into the fold. “That remains a huge chunk (of mosques) and suggestions (from the religious leaders) are sought on that,” said Mr. Mohi-ud-Din.
It’s a rare bid by the Waqf to bring uniformity in sermons, which otherwise would often drift towards global and local political issues in the past. Friday sermons delivered in all mosques in J&K have two parts, where a preacher delves upon a contemporary issue and also recites the sermons delivered by Prophet Muhammad. It is followed by congregational prayers attended in large numbers in J&K.
Delving into the mechanism, senior BJP leader and Board chairperson Syed Darakhshan Andrabi said, “Sermons are about faith, society and the future of this place. There will be no changes in ‘Khutba Rasool’ (sermons of the Prophet). However, for the greater good, the Imam and Khateebs (religious preachers) will speak on issues in one voice, whether it’s drugs, women, waywardness, women’s issues etc.”
She underlined that a committee of religious scholars would get to decide on the topics. “The chairperson and officials will have no role in it. The committee will decide what topics should be touched upon in the sermons,” said Ms. Andrabi.
Prominent religious scholars like Abdul Rashid Dawoodi and Maulana R. H Noorabadi also attended the meeting.

briefs.headline: India's economic story in fast lane, IMF projects 7% GDP growth for FY26 and FY27
briefs.deck: India is projected to maintain a robust growth rate of 7% in both 2026 and 2027, bolstered by strong domestic demand and a thriving services sector, according to the International Monetary Fund. Positive revisions from the World Bank and OECD highlight resilience amid consumption patterns. However, challenges such as rising energy prices and geopolitical tensions could impact this trajectory, yet…
briefs.bodyText:
India’s economy is expected to grow by 7% in both 2026 and 2027, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), keeping the country among the fastest-growing major economies despite growing uncertainties. According to the institution, strong domestic demand, robust services activity and favourable demographic trends are expected to support this growth.
India's growth prospects were supported by favourable demographic dynamics, a large and expanding domestic market, and continued structural reforms, even as higher oil prices posed a challenge.
“India stands out with upward revisions, reflecting sustained momentum and growing evidence of stronger growth potential supported by favorable demographic dynamics, a large and expanding domestic market, and continued structural reforms.”
The forecast comes amid a series of upgrades by global agencies after India's gross domestic product (GDP) grew 7.8% in the April-June quarter of the current financial year.
India holds its ground despite higher oil prices
The agency expects India to remain among the fastest-growing major economies, with domestic demand and services activity helping sustain momentum.
“India remains among the fastest-growing major economies, with growth in 2026 projected at 7.0 percent. 
This reflects stronger-than-expected momentum, supported by resilient domestic demand and robust services activity.”
It also highlighted how the Indian economy continued to expand despite rising oil prices. “India’s growth remained robust, underpinned by domestic demand and services, despite higher oil prices.”
The improved outlook follows the stronger-than-expected GDP growth recorded in the April-June quarter, prompting several global institutions, including the World Bank, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), S&P Global Ratings, Moody's Ratings, Fitch Ratings and the Asian Development Bank (ADB), to raise their growth estimates for India.
World Bank, OECD raise India growth forecasts
The World Bank raised its growth projection for India in 2026-27 to 7.1%, from 6.6% estimated earlier. The multilateral agency attributed the revision to strong domestic demand and exports, despite global headwinds. It expects the economy to grow by 7.2% in 2027-28.
The OECD has also increased its forecast for India's GDP growth in 2026-27 to 7.1%, from 6.3% projected in June. The revised estimate is higher than the 7% forecasts from S&P, Moody's and ADB, while Fitch expects growth of 6.9%.
Moody's Ratings raised its forecast for India's real GDP growth in FY27 to 7%, from 6%, citing the economy's resilience amid the Middle East conflict.
"Although we continue to expect India to grow faster than all other G-20 economies, as well as similarly rated emerging market sovereigns, risks remain," Moody’s said.
Expansion in the April-June quarter was supported by strong investment and manufacturing activity, which helped offset weakness in mining and consumer-facing services.
Global growth faces a more fragile outlook
While India has received a series of growth upgrades, the IMF has warned that the global economy's resilience is becoming increasingly fragile and uneven.
“The global economy remains resilient, but that resilience is becoming more fragile and more uneven. Growth is projected at 3.1% in 2026 and 3.4% in 2027, while inflation is expected to reach 4.7%, driven largely by higher energy and food prices.”
The global outlook also presents risks for India.
Higher crude oil and energy prices could fuel inflation and put pressure on household purchasing power. Below-normal monsoon rainfall could affect agricultural output and rural demand, while prolonged geopolitical tensions could disrupt supply chains and increase input costs.
Despite the upward revisions to India's growth projections, these factors remain among the risks flagged by agencies assessing the country's economic outlook.

briefs.headline: IMF slightly raises forecast for 2026 global growth to 3.1%, citing 'resilience' to shocks
briefs.deck: In its World Economic Outlook report, the Fund left its forecast for 2027 global growth unchanged at 3.4%
briefs.bodyText:
he International Monetary Fund on Tuesday (October 13, 2026) forecast global growth in 2026 would slow less than previously expected because of advanced economies’ “resilience” in the face of war-fuelled energy prices, but warned low-income countries remained vulnerable to the supply shock.
In its World Economic Outlook (WEO) released at the organization’s Annual Meetings in Bangkok, the IMF raised its 2026 global growth forecast by 0.1 percentage points to 3.1%, compared with 3.5% growth in 2025.
It warned that while many advanced economies have been buoyed by rising investment in artificial intelligence (AI) technology, poorer countries that are not benefiting from that boom face stark choices as they deal with high energy prices caused by the Iran war.
“The global economy has been resilient, but that resilience is under strain, with risks tilted to the downside,” Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF’s chief economist, told journalists in Bangkok.
With global debt-to-GDP ratios at sky-high levels, including in advanced economies, the IMF has called on governments to cut spending and manage borrowing — a difficult task for those in the developing world struggling with the Iran war shock.
“What we are advocating for is for policymakers to balance the near-term needs of inflation, and that involves food security, that involves energy security... while also keeping in mind the medium-term stability,” said Deniz Igan, chief of the IMF’s World Economic Studies division.
‘Bifurcated outlook’
The United States’ war on Iran, launched in February, has plunged the Middle East into violence and seen global energy prices skyrocket as a result of Tehran’s retaliation.
Prices of refined petroleum products remain between 70 and 95 percent above pre-war levels, putting pressure on countries dependent on energy imports for economic activity.
On Monday night, blasts resounded across Saudi Arabia’s capital as the war’s impact widens into that country, with Iran-backed Yemeni Houthi forces hitting oil facilities, tankers and transport hubs.
“A more prolonged disruption of production and transport in the Middle East could lead to” higher inflation and a drag on growth, said Tenreyro.
Energy-importing countries not exposed to the AI boom remain the most vulnerable, creating what the IMF termed a “bifurcated outlook” in its WEO report.
The report detailed that the twin economic forces of the war in Iran and the AI technology boom had created a “fragmented” world economy.
“Headwinds from a prolonged war and persistent geopolitical tensions could revive inflationary pressures, strain fiscal and external positions, and hit energy-importing and low-income countries hardest,” it said.
“At the same time, the current technology tailwind could stop abruptly if expectations about AI-related profits and productivity gains are reassessed, weakening investment and tightening financial conditions.”
Responding to AFP, Tenreyro said AI had been a major factor driving the world economy, accounting for almost half of the increase in global trade from 2023 to 2025.
Contraction here, growth there
The IMF’s split view of the world economy was evident in its specific projections.
The Middle East and Central Asia region -- exposed directly to the Iran war as Tehran targets Washington’s Gulf allies and the Houthi offensive against Saudi Arabia has picked up -- is expected to suffer a 0.3 percent contraction in 2026.
Saudi Arabia’s is one of the worst affected, with its economy projected to shrink 3.3 percent -- representing a 5.0 percentage points cut in the Fund’s forecast.
The IMF said the region is expected to bounce back quickly once the war is over, but there remains high uncertainty as to when that will be.
In advanced economies, growth fuelled by the AI boom and other factors remained strong.
The world’s advanced economies were forecast to grow 2.1 percent in 2026, with those in the AI supply chain such as Taiwan and South Korea posting significantly higher figures.
Growth in China, the world’s second-largest economy, was expected to slow, the IMF said, mainly because of weak domestic demand.
Global inflation remained set to accelerate to 4.7 percent in 2026, with effects spread across advanced and developing economies.
Call for action
Tenreyro warned that urgent action was required by all countries in the face of downside risks, and called on governments to only use temporary, targeted measures to help ease the burden on the public of high energy and other costs.
In lockstep, “monetary policy should remain firmly focused on price stability”, she added, indicating that interest rate hikes to curb high inflation were appropriate.
“The economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits,” she said. “The task ahead is to move from coping to rebuilding, restoring fiscal space and supply-side resilience.”

briefs.headline: Why does India need a trained workforce for elderly care?
briefs.deck: India’s 60-plus population is projected to touch 347 million by 2050, underscoring the need for a robust caregiving ecosystem; a formal training programme, building on existing small-scale initiatives, could promote gender parity in caregiving and recognise informal, unpaid family caregivers
briefs.bodyText:
Every day Sreeni wakes up at 4.30 am and checks on his mother. If she is unsteady on waking up, he will assist her to the raised toilet and wait outside as she independently uses it, assuring her that help is just outside. There is a schedule of medicines, clearly sorted and kept by her bedside. The BP monitor and the glucometer reassure him that everything is in the range for her age. He learnt it all by himself, one emergency visit after another to the hospital. Hip pain was ignored till it became a debilitating fracture, a sudden loss of consciousness detected as low sodium — each crisis was a hard lesson in the trial-and-error reality of informal caregiving. Every day millions like Sreeni wake up and perform their respective self-taught routines to take care of their parents or dependants.
As our country’s population ages over the next two decades, the topic of caregiving and the need for formal training for the task will assume larger dimensions, and this is precisely what the Budget 2026-27 has highlighted in a timely manner with the announcement of training of 1.5 lakh caregivers aligned to the National Skills Qualifications Framework.
The NITI Aayog’s August 2026 report “Reimagining Care: Strategies for Empowering Caregivers in Viksit Bharat@2047” frames caregiving as an economic activity rather than just welfare work, and this is the first time that such an intention is explicitly articulated by the Government at a national policy level, which indicates that the urgency has been acknowledged by policymakers.
Also Read: India’s growing elderly population needs an integrated care system, says report
To put it in perspective, India’s 60-plus population, estimated at approximately 149 million in 2022, is projected to touch 347 million by 2050, forming roughly 20.8% of the total population. Assuming NITI Aayog’s estimate that 10% of the population today is engaged in caregiving while being untrained and unpaid, the current total works out to about 146 million.
The planned 1.5 lakh formally trained workforce is just a drop in the ocean even by today’s requirements. The caregiving ecosystem will be at a serious juncture if we don’t plan now.
Gender parity in caregiving
For most of its history, India never needed a long-term care system because it had one: the joint family. Three generations under one roof was an insurance contract written in spirit and practised willingly. In the present scenario, with micro family units, most of the time, it is the housewives who take upon themselves the additional task of caregiving, having no formal training, learning by trial and sometimes serious error. Combined with the need to manage their own household chores, such situations increase household stress considerably. The aged who need assistance and the differently abled, about 26.8 million, are surviving, thanks to the love, care and affection of these unpaid, informal care givers.
An NSO survey has worked out that women, on average, spend 299 minutes per day on unpaid domestic work and caregiving, whereas for men it is only 97 minutes. What is required is an appreciation of the situation and the demands of caregiving being shouldered by both genders. A formal training programme, designed exclusively around caregiving, covering the detection of age-related events needing attention in the elderly, assessment of needs, continuous monitoring protocols, emergency care and psychological interventions, ideally attended by at least two family members, would improve the sharing of the duties and responsibilities.
Skilling and upskilling
If we need to have a large number of skilled, formally trained caregivers in a few years’ time, we need to start in earnest.
Two structures are functioning in India, albeit on a small scale and untested. Kudumbashree is a State mission based in Kerala that runs a network of self-help groups. It launched the K4 Care training programme in February 2024 under which its members qualify as certified geriatric/patient/disability care executives. Recent data shows that only 838 have completed the course, a rather slow progress. We can incentivise and accelerate the programme.
The other group is the ASHA workers for whom the NHSRC (National Health Systems Resource Centre) has prepared a Training Manual on Elderly Care, with training delivered via Ayushman Bharat Health and Wellness Centres. However, granular details as to the number of ASHA workers who have completed this training are not available publicly. A meaningful intervention here can have a positive impact.
Informal caregiving is not always physical, like mobility assistance or medicine management. Age-related cognitive decline — as seen in Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease — involves several emotional challenges as well. Any national curriculum must factor in geriatric mental health and behavioural management along with physical care protocols.
The way forward
There are millions of informal, unpaid family caregivers. We need to validate and upskill them into recognised caregivers.
Kudumbashree and ASHA workers who are formally trained, can serve as trainers to train more people, allowing the chain to continue. The National Caregiver Council (NCC), as envisaged in the NITI Aayog report, can act as an apex body. It can set benchmarks and supervise skill development, update training modules, standardise curricula, come out with useful FAQs and regulate and manage a national caregiver portal with a list of certified caregivers.
Transforming India’s care economy is an economic strategy waiting to be unlocked. By creating such a robust ecosystem, India can turn informal dedication into professional expertise with great economic value. For millions like Sreeni, being recognised as a caregiver for the elderly and being trained formally to deal with the associated challenges bring dignity to the relationship.
Just as India is recognised the world over for its healthcare nursing professionals, its approach to managing the challenges of elderly care too could be adopted as the compassionate alternative to the many models being practised globally. The fact that this has been announced as a Budget item is just the seed, and operationalising it at the ground level is where the final success lies.
(T.C. Suseel Kumar a former Managing Director and R. Sudhakar is a former Executive Director, LIC. Views expressed are personal.)

briefs.headline: Trump attacks immigrants from Somalia and Haiti while rallying in Ohio for Republican candidates
briefs.deck: If you want to stop Ohio from being plundered, ransacked and destroyed like Minnesota is being destroyed, we're going to stop it, says U.S. President Donald Trump
briefs.bodyText:
U.S. President Donald Trump on Monday (October 12, 2026) tried to boost Senator Jon Husted's re-election campaign by attacking two groups of Black immigrants during a rally in Ohio, where an organisation with Republican ties began promoting a socialist candidate over Democratic nominee Sherrod Brown.
Mr. Trump also gave a shoutout to Rep. Max Miller, the Republican congressman who refused to stop running for reelection after facing accusations of domestic abuse, pointing him out in the audience.
“Thank you, Max, for coming,” Mr. Trump said. “Thank you. Very good.”
Mr. Trump focused, however, on a favourite issue — immigration. Mr. Trump has long targeted Minnesota's large population of Somali immigrants, and on Monday he linked that group to Haitians in Springfield, Ohio. During a presidential debate two years ago, Mr. Trump falsely accused the latter group of eating pets. Referencing those allegations Monday, Mr. Trump said “I was right” and boasted that Haitians were being driven out of the country by his administration's policies.
“If you want to stop Ohio from being plundered, ransacked and destroyed like Minnesota is being destroyed, we're going to stop it,” Mr. Trump said. “Just like we did with Springfield, we're going to stop it, we're not going to let it happen.”
Mr. Trump's remarks came on the same day Homeland Security agents searched the Washington home of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar, a Somali immigrant who represents a Minnesota district.
The president visited Youngstown less than a week after rallying in Dayton. The intense focus on Ohio, a State Mr. Trump won by 11 percentage points, shows the challenging environment Republicans are navigating in the midterms amid the Iran war and lingering inflation. In addition to the Senate contest, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy is locked in a close governor's race with Democrat Amy Acton.
The rally was also a reminder of the extent Trump is willing to go to boost his allies — he announced a new submarine component manufacturing center will be located in nearby Cleveland during the rally — and his persistent focus on Black immigrants.
Back in 2018, Trump privately complained about immigrants from countries like Haiti — using an expletive to describe them — and wondered why the United States couldn't get more migrants from places like Norway. The statement was condemned as racist and Mr. Trump denied making it at the time.
But Mr. Trump admitted using the phrase last year, and his second administration has focused on restricting immigration and barring any refugees except white South Africans.
During the rally, he celebrated what he contended was an exodus of Haitians out of Springfield. The Trump administration ended a program that allowed more than 350,000 Haitians to stay in the country legally, which some of the roughly 15,000 Haitians who arrived in Springfield, population 60,000, in recent years.
“They're getting their town back,” Trump said about the original residents of Springfield, as he also stood by his debunked statement at the 2024 presidential debate that the Haitians were eating local pets. That claim was based on a secondhand Facebook post whose author deleted it and apologized, saying she had no evidence it was true.
Mr. Trump devoted even more time to insulting immigrants from Somalia, where he claimed that people were “low IQ” and “don't have pants to wear.”
Mr. Trump's main goal was to boost Husted, who was appointed to replace Vice President JD Vance in the Senate in 2024 and faces a tough challenge from Brown, a longtime senator who lost his seat to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024.
The presidential visit came after mailers, sponsored by Enough Promises Ohio PAC, began arriving in voters' mailboxes in recent days. They promote independent candidate Greg Levy over Brown with messages such as “Join the Revolution” and “Send a Worker to the Senate.” Levy describes himself as “Socialist running for the U.S. Senate to represent Ohio in 2026” on his X account.
Levy condemned the fliers for falsely impersonating his campaign and engaging in “dirty tricks” designed to mislead voters. He said he is considering legal action.
“This is a highly undemocratic practice and does a disservice to voters in Ohio and throughout the country,” he wrote on X.

stories.headline: Police crack down on anti-SIR protesters in Bengaluru, detain 100
stories.deck: The police threatened journalists covering the protest and ordered them to leave the spot, while three photographers were manhandled, despite repeatedly identifying themselves as members of the Press.
stories.bodyText:
Protesters who tried to march to the Chief Electoral Officer (CEO), Karnataka’s office in Bengaluru on Monday, to condemn the Delhi Police’s treatment of demonstrators protesting against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), faced similar heavy-handedness from the Bengaluru City Police, with at least 100 people detained, and students, lawyers, and women protesters allegedly manhandled.
Senior journalist and activist Aakar Patel was also detained. The police threatened journalists covering the protest and ordered them to leave the spot, while three photographers were manhandled, despite repeatedly identifying themselves as members of the Press.
Several protesters, most of them students, were forcibly pushed into buses by police personnel, many of whom were not in uniform. Male police personnel were seen forcing women protesters into buses, with the police arguing that the protesters would return to the spot if they were released.
A senior police officer, however, defended the actions, arguing that the police did not know about the protest and were taken by surprise. Given only Freedom Park is the designated protest site, they were bound to detain protesters outside that venue. He also admitted that since the police were not aware, the force included mostly male personnel.
The protest was organised by Left student and youth organisations across Karnataka, which planned marches to the CEO’s office in Bengaluru and Deputy Commissioners’ offices in other districts. They demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the scrapping of SIR of electoral rolls.
In Bengaluru, the protesters assembled near K.R. Circle, a few metres from the CEO’s office, and planned to submit a memorandum to the CEO. However, the police detained them before they could march to the office.
Akshay M. Hakay, DCP Central, said “a group of protesters assembled near K.R. Circle, without permission or prior intimation. This is in contrary to the High Court’s directions of protesting at designated places. Initially, they were requested to relocate to Freedom Park, but they did not comply and hence, were taken into preventive custody in accordance with law, and subsequently released,” he said, adding that the police acted with due restraint and sensitivity in the prevailing circumstances.
In their memorandum to the CEO, the protesters said they had lost faith in the SIR process, pointing that the exercise is leading to the denial of voting rights, arbitrary deletion of names, procedural irregularities, and a lack of transparency and accountability.
They also questioned the handling of cases in which FIRs had been registered over bulk filing of Form 7 applications, asking why Electoral Registration Officers had not filed complaints yet.
The groups demanded immediate cancellation of the SIR, the resignation of Mr. Kumar, restoration of the January 2025 electoral rolls, and safeguards against arbitrary deletions in any future revision. The groups said they would protest until the CEC resigns.

stories.headline: Karnataka high court strikes down 56% quota as 'unconstitutional'
stories.deck: Karnataka high court ruled that the law increasing reservations for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes is unconstitutional. The court found the law violated the 50% reservation ceiling set by the Supreme Court. Key issues included lack of consultation with relevant constitutional commissions before enacting the legislation. The judgment followed petitions challenging the law’s validity and the…
stories.bodyText:
BENGALURU: In a setback to the state govt, Karnataka high court Monday struck down as “constitutionally impermissible” the law that raised overall reservations for Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs) to 56% against the 50% ceiling laid down by Supreme Court.
A division bench of Chief Justice Vibhu Bakhru and Justice KS Hemalekha ruled Section 3 of Karnataka Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Reservation of Seats in Educational Institutions and Appointment of Posts in the Services under the State) Act, 2022, was unconstitutional as it pushed total reservation beyond 50%, violating Articles 14 and 15 of the Constitution. The bench also struck down Section 4 of the Act for violating Articles 14 and 16.
The law, which was pushed into effect during the BJP govt led by 
Basavaraj Bommai
, increased reservation for SCs from 15% to 17% and for STs from 3% to 7%, while the quota for backward classes remained at 32%.
The verdict came on petitions filed by Raichur-based social worker Mahendra Kumar Mitra and HR Sagar and two others.
One of the key grounds for striking down the law was the state govt’s failure to consult the National Commission for Scheduled Castes and the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes before enacting the legislation.
The bench observed that reservation policy was a major policy matter and consultation with the two constitutional bodies was mandatory under Articles 338(9) and 338A(9) of the Constitution. Merely writing to the commissions after the law had been enacted could not be treated as meaningful consultation, it said.
The court noted that the letters relied on by the state govt were dated Dec 10, 2025, and Jan 20, 2026 — nearly three years after the Act was enacted and after its validity had been challenged before the high court.
The bench rejected the argument that the findings of Justice H N Nagamohandas Commission justified exceeding the 50% reservation ceiling. While the commission’s conclusion that certain communities remained marginalised and had not adequately benefited from reservation could support a case for internal reservation, it did not justify breaching the overall ceiling, the court said.
The bench reiterated that the 50% rule was intended to strike a balance between affirmative action under Articles 15(4) and 16(4) and the principles of equality under Articles 15(1) and 16(1).
The court had clarified that appointments arising from recruitment processes already underway would remain subject to the final outcome of the cases. Appointment and promotion letters were required to expressly state this condition, and candidates could not claim any equitable rights if the enhanced reservation was ultimately struck down.

stories.headline: Gayathri Chandrashekar to portray 14 characters in Ramayana production at Mysuru Dasara
stories.bodyText:
Bharatanatyam dancer Gayathri Chandrashekar has performed Sri Rama Charitham for over four decades, portraying 14 characters from the Ramayana in a solo performance that traces Lord Rama’s journey. This year, she will present the one-hour production during the 
Mysuru Dasara
 festivities on October 13. Originally choreographed by her teacher as a 20-minute piece when Gayathri was just 12, the production has evolved over the years into what she describes as an “experience of a lifetime”.
‘Sri Rama Charitham has evolved with me’
The distinctive feature of Sri Rama Charitham is that Gayathri portrays every character herself, from Rama, Sita and Lakshmana to Ravana, Hanuman and Shabari. Rather than changing costumes for each role, she relies on expressions, body language and movement to bring each character to life. Her students will join her in selected portions of the production, which culminates in Rama’s coronation. “I have performed this many times. It started off as a small 20-minute Padam when I was a kid, choreographed by my teacher. Over the years, it has evolved with me. I have made it into a piece that is almost an hour and 15 minutes long,” she says.
While many classical dance performances during Navaratri focus on Goddess Durga, Gayathri believes the story of Lord Rama is equally relevant to the festivities, which also celebrate his triumph over Ravana. The timeless appeal of the epic, she says, helps audiences connect with its characters, even if they are unfamiliar with Bharatanatyam. “Ramayana is evergreen. The character has to be brought out in such a way that the audience is able to understand the story and relate to it,” she says.
‘Switching between characters comes from within; it doesn’t need costumes’
Moving between divine, demonic and human characters in a matter of seconds requires years of training and a deep understanding of their personalities. Gayathri relies on subtle shifts in posture, expression and energy to make each transition distinct. “From the body language of a Rakshasa to a God, to Sita, who has a completely feminine energy, to Hanuman, who embodies valour, the characterisation has worked in my mind for many years,” she says.
This year’s performance holds special significance for Gayathri as she presents Sri Rama Charitham at Mysuru Dasara for the first time, at Jaganmohan Palace.

stories.headline: Stormwater carrying sewage water enters recently restored Sampigehalli Lake during rain
stories.deck: While conservationists and residents are working with the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) officials to find a permanent solution, concerns remain over sewage entering the lake, fish deaths due to sewage water entry, and the lack of a reliable power supply for equipment installed to improve water quality.
stories.bodyText:
Sampigehalli Lake, which was recently restored, continues to receive sewage water, with the problem escalating during heavy rain, as drainage problems around the lake are yet to be fully addressed.
While conservationists and residents are working with the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) officials to find a permanent solution, concerns remain over sewage entering the lake, fish deaths due to sewage water entry, and the lack of a reliable power supply for equipment installed to improve water quality.
Ravindra, secretary of the Venkateshwar Nagar residents’ association, said residents had complained in the past about sewage being discharged directly into the lake at night. Following their protests, a pipeline was laid to carry the discharge to the other end of the lake. He said, “However, we continue to notice black water and waste along the lake’s edges.” As the lake is closed at night, residents cannot confirm whether sewage is still being discharged directly into it.
Mr. Ravindra said the problem could also be linked to sewage treatment plants (STPs) at nearby apartment complexes getting flooded during heavy rain, allowing contaminated water to enter the lake. “But either way, this is resulting in heavy stench and posing health concerns.”
Speaking to The Hindu, the residents pointed to problems with the drainage system around the lake. The catchment area has been reduced, leaving less space for rainwater to flow into the lake. As a quick-fix, a mud barrier was created, that has temporarily blocked one of the inlets, but residents fear that it may not hold when there is heavy rain.
They demand a permanent solution with separate systems to carry sewage and rainwater.
Residents argue that this is only one such inflow that poses a problem during every spell of heavy rain, when water from a nearby apartment complex is usually
M. Subhadra, a resident and adjunct fellow at Ashoka Trust for Research in Ecology and the Environment (ATREE), which was involved in the restoration of the lake, said that while the situation had since stabilised, the members are still finding a permanent solution to the inflow.
GBA officials said flooding in several areas had been linked to ongoing project work, disconnected stormwater drains, low-lying areas and local structural conditions. They said they were in touch with those affected to work towards a permanent solution.

briefs.headline: Garba is a celebration, an opportunity to connect: Ashmit Patel
briefs.deck: Ashmit Patel brings Gujarati beats, fresh mixes and festive energy to Bangalore Times’ Garba Nite
briefs.bodyText:
Music is more than a profession for actor and DJ Ashmit Patel. It is a way to connect with people, find creative satisfaction and, most importantly, make them happy. This Navaratri, he brings that energy to Bangalore Times’ Garba Nite on October 18 at Bhartiya Mall of Bengaluru, blending traditional Garba sounds with his own musical flavour.
“I’m super excited because it’s been a while since I played in Bengaluru, and even longer since I’ve done a Garba event. Me being a Patel, the Dandiya-Garba connection runs quite deep. It’ll be nice to connect with my roots and play some traditional music along with some interesting mixes I’ve prepared for the evening,” he says.
Over the years, Garba has travelled beyond its Gujarati roots to become a vibrant celebration that brings people together across communities. Ashmit says its appeal lies as much in the spirit of togetherness as in the music, dance and colourful attire.
“It’s an opportunity for youngsters to come together, dance, enjoy and connect. It’s so colourful, and the outfits too are beautiful. The styling, cuts and colours are so vibrant. Some of these dancers are incredible. It’s almost like a martial art, the way they do it,” he says.
‘DJing is like theatre because the response is instant’
Ashmit began DJing in 2014, after the release of Jai Ho, when he decided to take a break from acting rather than sign up for projects simply to stay busy. 
“DJing was something I had aspired to do since I was a teenager. It’s been interesting and fun to discover my own sound, understand what kind of music I enjoy playing and see how different crowds across the country and the world react to it,” he says.
“When you’re DJing, you have a live audience in front of you, so you know if what you’re doing is hitting the spot. Sometimes, you have to adjust on the fly, change your music or your energy if you’re not connecting with the crowd,” he shares.
Whether performing as celebrity DJ 
Ashmit Patel
 or playing electronic music under the name Ashiva, connecting with his audience remains central to his work. While the celebrity tag may draw people in, he finds greater satisfaction in seeing them respond to the music and enjoy themselves.
“When people come to see Ashmit Patel, the actor who is a DJ, there’s also a bit of a show that I’m putting on. But beyond the selfies and handshakes, when people dance to your tunes, have a great night and genuinely enjoy themselves, that’s even more gratifying. For me, it’s about being creatively satisfied and being happy with the way my life is. I just want to be happy, content and joyful. I want to spread love and happiness, and I want to make sure that people I interact with have a pleasant experience,” he adds.

briefs.headline: Apartment owners await new law, meet Karnataka governor
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 A Bangalore Apartments Federation (BAF) delegation met governor Thaawar Chand Gehlot Friday and submitted a representation, highlighting the importance of the proposed new apartment law in securing apartment ownership, protecting common areas and ensuring accountable community governance.
Karnataka Apartment Ownership and Management Bill (KAOMA), 2026, passed by the legislature, is awaiting assent from governor.
Several residents are eager to see the ownership and management rules take effect, which will define the rights and duties of apartment owners.
“Apartment ownership should mean more than owning four walls; it should include meaningful rights over the common property shared by all owners,” says Satish Mallya, president of BAF.
Meanwhile, a few home buyer associations said Rera already requires the promoter to execute registered conveyance and transfer undivided proportionate title in common areas to the association of allottees or competent authority, as applicable.
However, the challenge is timely compliance and enforcement, noted Mallya.
Vikram Rai, former president of BAF, said that for older apartments like Brigade Millennium, where he lives, which have been registered under Karnataka Societies Registration Act (KSRA), the biggest advantage that KAOMA brings is the automatic recognition as an apartment association, while many courts have effectively rejected the legitimacy of KSRA for apartments.
“Also, the fact that KAOMA amply clarifies that the land and common areas of an apartment complex collectively belong to all owners in proportion to their undivided rights and gives the association the legitimate right to manage, maintain and administer the property, including statutory rights for assessment and recovery of maintenance charges, is very significant,” he added.
However, Dhananjaya Padmanabhachar, convener of Karnataka Home Buyers Forum (KHBF), said the KAOMA bill omits essential provisions for transferring common areas to registered associations. This omission contradicts the requirements set forth in Rera, he said.

briefs.headline: Priest collecting flowers killed in leopard attack in Karnataka
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: A 55-year-old priest died after a leopard attacked him inside a farm near Magadi, Ramanagara-Bengaluru South early Monday morning.
The deceased is Shivaswamy, a resident of Kalludevanahalli and the main priest with Mahadeshwara temple in his village.
According to police, Shivaswamy had left home around 5.45am to collect flowers for his temple from the agricultural field, around 400 metres away from home. According to villagers, it was Shivaswamy’s routine to collect flowers for the temple by predawn.
However, by 7am, Shivaswamy was found lying in a pool of blood by a milkman who alerted the villagers. “At first, the milkman wondered why Poojarappa (Shivaswamy) was lying with his face down. When went near, milkman saw blood oozing out from the priest’s neck and abdomen. There were pug marks near the body. The milkman realised that an animal had attacked and killed the priest,” Magadi police told 
TOI
.
Later, the forest officials visited the spot and confirmed that the pug marks belonged to a male leopard. “Shivaswamy had collected a basketful of flowers when he was attacked. The flowers were scattered near the body,” police said.

briefs.headline: Man, 65, walks on Bengaluru Metro track, disrupts Purple Line trains
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: Namma Metro services on Purple Line between Vijayanagar and Challaghatta were disrupted for 15 minutes Monday evening after a 65-year-old man got onto the tracks between Deepanjali Nagar and Mysore Road stations.
The disruption occurred between 8:15pm and 8:30pm, during which a few trains were held up. Normal services on the entire Purple Line resumed at 8:30 pm.
A police officer said, “The 65-year-old man, identified as Somanna, entered the tracks at Mysuru Road station, under the jurisdiction of Byatarayanapura police station, and attempted to walk towards Deepanjali Nagar station. Metro staff rescued him and no one was injured. An approaching train was briefly halted during the incident, after which services resumed as usual.”

briefs.headline: Sadahalli underpass set to ease Bengaluru airport road traffic
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: To eliminate the last traffic signal on the main carriageway of Ballari Road connecting Kempegowda International Airport, National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) has begun construction of an underpass at Sadahalli Junction.
NHAI is constructing the 750-metre-long, six-lane underpass at a cost of ₹35 crore. A press release said the project is expected to be completed by mid-2027.
Traffic police said no diversions have been imposed at the junction so far. Besides airport traffic, motorists coming from Sadahalli and nearby localities and travelling towards the city or Devanahalli will be able to use the overpass at the junction.
A traffic police officer said they had been informed that NHAI would take up work in phases, considering high traffic volume.
Cut-and-cover road works at IAF Station after Aero Show
NHAI has stated that cut-and-cover work for the service road near Indian Air Force (IAF) station in Yelahanka will begin after the Aero India show in Feb 2027. According to NHAI, service road works near the IAF area are being executed in phases.
Phase I, covering the initial 240-metre stretch between IAF Gates 1 and 2, along with associated utility and compound works, has been completed.
Phase II, covering the stretch between Gates 2 and 3, is in progress, with completion targeted for Dec 2026. The service road on the domestic side, between Gates 5 and 6, will be taken up after Bengaluru Metro Rail Corporation hands over encumbrance-free land.

briefs.headline: After public outcry, long-neglected Bengaluru road gets overnight fix
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: Sustained media campaign, non-stop citizen activism and local leaders’ persistence — this is the right blend to fix a road overnight that was neglected for years. Commuters on Kanteerava Studio Road had to endure potholes, dust, traffic snarls and a crater that turned every ride into an obstacle course. Now, the stretch between Surana College and Nandini Layout has been asphalted in a dramatic turnaround.
A big relief to motorists, but it has also raised an important question: if a road can be fixed in hours, why did commuters have to wait so long? The road took its share of spotlight last week after heavy rain caused a section of the carriageway to collapse, leaving behind a huge crater. The situation drew attention when a video clip of a heated exchange between a commuter, identified as Vivek C, and Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) officials during a road inspection went viral on social media. Congress functionary Kusuma H, too, pressured civic officials to act without excuses.
What followed was a swift response from Bengaluru West City Corporation (BWCC). Within days of public uproar, workers moved in to resurface the battered stretch, completing the work — on a Saturday night.
TOI had reported on the matter on October 9
As 
TOI
 reported earlier, the road’s repair had been held up for nearly a year with Bengaluru Smart Infrastructure (B-Smile) proposing to convert it into a white-topped road while motorists suffered on a daily basis. “It took so many messages and repeated letters to higher authorities. And all it took was less than a night to give us a good road,” said Deepak Gowda, a regular user of the stretch, thanking 
TOI
 for highlighting the issue. “This is all we have been waiting for. 
It’s not really difficult for our corporations to build roads; it is the choice they make.”
Shwetha, another commuter, said the improvement was immediately noticeable, although she remained unsure about the road’s long-term quality. “Earlier, there was so much dust and congestion. With the road now properly paved, vehicles move smoothly,” she said.
Yet, residents have a concern: if the asphalt is of poor quality or if utility agencies dig it up to lay cables, pipelines or other infrastructure, what happens? For now, that’s a story for another day.

briefs.headline: Karnataka Prisons Department struggles to find ‘suitable cell’ for Prajwal Revanna
briefs.deck: The Department has agreed in principle to the police’s recommendation to transfer Prajwal and 11 other prisoners after they were caught using mobile phones inside the prison.
briefs.bodyText:
Prajwal Revanna, convicted former MP, has put the Karnataka’s Department of Prisons and Correctional Services in a fix, with officials struggling to identify a “suitable cell” to shift him from Parappana Agrahara Central Prison in Bengaluru following a recommendation by the city police to do so.
The Department has agreed in principle to the police’s recommendation to transfer Prajwal and 11 other prisoners after they were caught using mobile phones inside the prison. The police have recommended that they be shifted to separate facilities, citing concerns that they could influence witnesses or hamper the investigation.
The Parappana Agrahara police had also taken Prajwal into custody for questioning about the source of the phones. Prison officials allegedly involved in the episode have been suspended.
However, the Prisons Department has since been struggling to identify a suitable facility to accommodate Prajwal while ensuring adequate security.
The irony is that Parappana Agrahara Central Prison, one of the largest prisons in the State and equipped with extensive security infrastructure, has apparently failed to prevent the alleged unauthorised use of phones by inmates. The latest episode has also raised questions about prison surveillance and the ability of influential prisoners to maintain networks from behind bars.
The department had initially considered shifting Prajwal to Hindalga Prison in Belagavi but dropped the plan after prison authorities expressed concerns over security arrangements.
Director General of Prisons and Correctional Services Alok Kumar said the proposed transfer was being reconsidered in consultation with the authorities concerned.
The Department is now exploring alternatives to ensure that the transfer, if carried out, does not compromise security or the ongoing investigation.

briefs.headline: Registrar of Societies can’t adjudicate civil disputes amongst members of clubs: Karnataka High Court
briefs.bodyText:
The High Court of Karnataka has issued guidelines on the exercise of power to conduct enquiries by the Registrar of Societies, while ruling that the statutory power cannot be used to adjudicate private civil disputes between members of clubs registered under the Karnataka Societies Registration Act (KSR Act), 1960.
Justice Suraj Govindaraj issued the directions while partly allowing a petition filed by the Cosmopolitan Club, Jayanagar.
Making a distinction
The court drew a clear distinction between the statutory power of the Registrar under Section 25 of the KSR Act to examine a society’s “constitution, working and financial condition” and the adjudication of private disputes.
While the Registrar can investigate genuine financial irregularities or statutory violations, he cannot assume the role of a civil court to decide which rival faction has the better right to control the management or hold office, the court said.
While issuing general guidelines for the Registrar to exercise power under Section 25 of the Act, the court directed that the Registrar must independently apply his mind before initiating a suo motu enquiry, rather than acting automatically on a complaint. The notice must specify with reasonable clarity which aspect of the society’s constitution, working or finances is being examined, the court said.
No parallel adjudication
Crucially, the court ruled that the Registrar cannot undertake a parallel adjudication of issues already pending before a civil court. However, the court clarified that the mere pendency of a civil suit does not bar the Registrar from conducting a genuine financial enquiry. The Registrar is permitted to examine financial irregularities and misappropriation of funds, as these fall squarely within the statutory field of Section 25. The court also cautioned against the use of open-ended clauses such as “other irregularities”, stating that such clauses cannot confer unlimited jurisdiction.
In the case of the petitioner club, the court found that the Registrar had indulged in an enquiry into certain issues pending before the civil court in pending suits and quashed the notice dated December 18, 2025, issued by an Enquiry Officer, which had initiated an enquiry into nine charges against the club. The charges included the suspension of office-bearers, the validity of elections, amendments to bye-laws and the opening of bank accounts.
The court directed the Registrar to issue a fresh notice to the petitioner club, confined strictly to matters within the statutory framework, excluding issues that require adjudication of private civil rights and subjects related to pending suits.

stories.headline: IMF upgrades 2026 growth forecast but warns of ‘split’ outlook
stories.deck: In its World Economic Outlook report, the Fund left its forecast for 2027 global growth unchanged at 3.4%
stories.bodyText:
he International Monetary Fund on Tuesday (October 13, 2026) forecast global growth in 2026 would slow less than previously expected because of advanced economies’ “resilience” in the face of war-fuelled energy prices, but warned low-income countries remained vulnerable to the supply shock.
In its World Economic Outlook (WEO) released at the organization’s Annual Meetings in Bangkok, the IMF raised its 2026 global growth forecast by 0.1 percentage points to 3.1%, compared with 3.5% growth in 2025.
It warned that while many advanced economies have been buoyed by rising investment in artificial intelligence (AI) technology, poorer countries that are not benefiting from that boom face stark choices as they deal with high energy prices caused by the Iran war.
“The global economy has been resilient, but that resilience is under strain, with risks tilted to the downside,” Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF’s chief economist, told journalists in Bangkok.
With global debt-to-GDP ratios at sky-high levels, including in advanced economies, the IMF has called on governments to cut spending and manage borrowing — a difficult task for those in the developing world struggling with the Iran war shock.
“What we are advocating for is for policymakers to balance the near-term needs of inflation, and that involves food security, that involves energy security... while also keeping in mind the medium-term stability,” said Deniz Igan, chief of the IMF’s World Economic Studies division.
‘Bifurcated outlook’
The United States’ war on Iran, launched in February, has plunged the Middle East into violence and seen global energy prices skyrocket as a result of Tehran’s retaliation.
Prices of refined petroleum products remain between 70 and 95 percent above pre-war levels, putting pressure on countries dependent on energy imports for economic activity.
On Monday night, blasts resounded across Saudi Arabia’s capital as the war’s impact widens into that country, with Iran-backed Yemeni Houthi forces hitting oil facilities, tankers and transport hubs.
“A more prolonged disruption of production and transport in the Middle East could lead to” higher inflation and a drag on growth, said Tenreyro.
Energy-importing countries not exposed to the AI boom remain the most vulnerable, creating what the IMF termed a “bifurcated outlook” in its WEO report.
The report detailed that the twin economic forces of the war in Iran and the AI technology boom had created a “fragmented” world economy.
“Headwinds from a prolonged war and persistent geopolitical tensions could revive inflationary pressures, strain fiscal and external positions, and hit energy-importing and low-income countries hardest,” it said.
“At the same time, the current technology tailwind could stop abruptly if expectations about AI-related profits and productivity gains are reassessed, weakening investment and tightening financial conditions.”
Responding to AFP, Tenreyro said AI had been a major factor driving the world economy, accounting for almost half of the increase in global trade from 2023 to 2025.
Contraction here, growth there
The IMF’s split view of the world economy was evident in its specific projections.
The Middle East and Central Asia region -- exposed directly to the Iran war as Tehran targets Washington’s Gulf allies and the Houthi offensive against Saudi Arabia has picked up -- is expected to suffer a 0.3 percent contraction in 2026.
Saudi Arabia’s is one of the worst affected, with its economy projected to shrink 3.3 percent -- representing a 5.0 percentage points cut in the Fund’s forecast.
The IMF said the region is expected to bounce back quickly once the war is over, but there remains high uncertainty as to when that will be.
In advanced economies, growth fuelled by the AI boom and other factors remained strong.
The world’s advanced economies were forecast to grow 2.1 percent in 2026, with those in the AI supply chain such as Taiwan and South Korea posting significantly higher figures.
Growth in China, the world’s second-largest economy, was expected to slow, the IMF said, mainly because of weak domestic demand.
Global inflation remained set to accelerate to 4.7 percent in 2026, with effects spread across advanced and developing economies.
Call for action
Tenreyro warned that urgent action was required by all countries in the face of downside risks, and called on governments to only use temporary, targeted measures to help ease the burden on the public of high energy and other costs.
In lockstep, “monetary policy should remain firmly focused on price stability”, she added, indicating that interest rate hikes to curb high inflation were appropriate.
“The economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits,” she said. “The task ahead is to move from coping to rebuilding, restoring fiscal space and supply-side resilience.”
