stories.headline: Oil prices hold near $105 per barrel as Trump eases sanctions on Russian fuel
stories.deck: Oil prices fell on Tuesday after increasing nearly $2 a barrel the previous session. Concerns over energy supply disruptions from ongoing conflicts in the Middle East influenced market sentiment. Meanwhile, US sanctions on Russian fuel were temporarily lifted, allowing for additional diesel supply. OPEC revised its demand growth forecast downward, indicating overcapacity in the market.
stories.bodyText:
Oil prices edged lower on Tuesday after rising by nearly $2 a barrel in the previous session, as traders weighed the risks to supplies from attacks on Saudi Arabia against the prospect of additional diesel supplies from Russia.
West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude was trading at $92.84 a barrel, down $0.90, or 0.96%, while Brent crude fell $1.01, or 0.95%, to $105.60 a barrel. This comes after Brent futures had settled at $106.65 a barrel on Monday, their highest level since September 15.
Oil markets have found some relief after US President Donald Trump said that Russia has agreed to supply diesel to global markets. The US administation temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel, which were designed to deprive Moscow of revenue for its war on Ukraine.
These additional supplies could ease tightness in global fuel markets and temper some of the supply concerns that have supported crude prices in recent weeks.
However, lawmakers from both parties in the US complained that Trump's agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin appeared to violate US law barring imports of Russian energy until Moscow ends its aggression against Ukraine.
Concerns about the vulnerability of energy infrastructure and shipping lanes in the Gulf continued to weigh on market sentiment after Iran-aligned Houthis struck Riyadh's international airport over the weekend. 
Attacks on tankers were also reported near the Strait of Hormuz.
The incidents threatened to derail the recovery in Middle East supplies seen in September, reinforcing concerns about further disruptions along one of the world's most important energy transit routes.
Ministers of OPEC and non-OPEC Participating Countries in the Declaration of Cooperation said shipping and insurance costs had surged to unprecedented levels, exceeding one-third of the commodity value. The higher costs were impeding the efficient movement of crude oil and petroleum products.
OPEC has also lowered its forecast for oil demand growth this year to 400,000 barrels per day (bpd), from 1.4 million bpd at the start of the year, reflecting developments throughout the year, the organisation's secretary general, Haitham Al Ghais, said on Monday, as cited by Reuters.
Meanwhile, Goldman Sachs said that brent crude prices could fall to the $60s per barrel in 2027 if oil production in the Persian Gulf recovers faster than expected. However, the investment bank warned that further escalation in the region could push prices significantly higher.
The bank said Brent could decline to the $60s if average oil output in the Gulf in 2027 rises by 1 million bpd above February 2026 levels.
“A faster recovery in Mideast output and/or a faster erosion of the risk premium are the most likely potential triggers of price downside,” Goldman Sachs said.
Continued adjustments in Middle East oil supplies would eventually bring crude prices down but renewed escalation in the region remained a significant risk that could push prices higher.
Now, the Middle East conflict has continued disrupt energy supplies for over seven months now, rattling oil markets and pushing prices high. However, even with the ongoing tensions, the spike is far lower than the $126 per barrel seen earlier during the crisis.

stories.headline: ADNOC open to further long-term LPG deals with India, sees India among most important energy markets: Acting CEO, Marketing
stories.deck: ADNOC supplied more than 500,000 barrels of crude a day to India in 2025, “almost one in ten barrels of [India’s] crude imports”. The company is exploring opportunities with ISPRL to expand storage of crude oil, LNG and LPG, including strategic reserves
stories.bodyText:
The Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) is open to further long-term liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) supply agreements with India and sees significant potential to deepen cooperation across crude oil, liquefied natural gas (LNG), naphtha, trading, shipping and strategic storage, Nasser Omair Al Muhairi, its Acting CEO (downstream industry, marketing and trading business) told The Hindu in an exclusive interaction.
“By combining [ADNOC’s] supply, trading and shipping capabilities, ADNOC is well positioned to provide Indian customers with reliable long-term LPG access, greater flexibility and enhanced energy security,” he said..
Mr. Al Muhairi described India as one of ADNOC’s most important energy markets.
Building on LPG supply agreement
Indian Oil had signed a strategic collaboration agreement with ADNOC in May during Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit to the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The agreement seeks to expand LPG supply and trading opportunities, including through ADNOC’s global trading unit, and potentially pave the way for a long-term sale and purchase agreement, building on the LPG term contract in place since 2023.
Mr. Al Muhairi said ADNOC’s “reliability, operational resilience and proximity” to key demand centres positioned it as a trusted partner in meeting India’s growing energy needs.
India among top energy markets
ADNOC supplied more than 500,000 barrels of crude oil a day to India in 2025, accounting for “almost one in ten barrels of [India’s] crude imports”, Mr. Al Muhairi said. The company is also among India’s leading suppliers of LNG and naphtha.
“Building on this foundation, we see significant opportunities to deepen cooperation across crude, LNG, LPG, naphtha, trading, shipping and strategic storage,” he said.
ADNOC’s ambition, he added, extended beyond supplying more energy to Indian customers to providing “greater security and flexibility while supporting investment and growth across the energy value chain.”
Expanding supply capacity
Mr. Al Muhairi said that ADNOC is working to increase its oil production capacity to five million barrels a day by 2027. It is also expanding domestic gas production and broadening access to global LNG supplies.
“Recent market conditions have reinforced the value of this integrated approach, with logistics and export infrastructure helping maintain reliable and flexible supply during periods of disruption,” Mr. Al Muhairi said.
Strategic storage plans
ADNOC is also exploring opportunities with Indian Strategic Petroleum Reserves Ltd. (ISPRL) to expand storage of crude oil, LNG and LPG, including strategic reserves.
“Our (ADNOC’s) immediate priority is advancing commercial and regulatory work with Indian Strategic Petroleum Reserves Limited (ISPRL) to determine capacities, investment and timelines,” Mr. Al Muhairi said.
The collaboration envisages increasing ADNOC’s crude oil storage capacity in India to as much as 30 million barrels. This includes the existing 5.86 million barrels of storage in Mangaluru and potential new facilities in Visakhapatnam and Chandikhol.
The two sides are also exploring the possibility of storing crude oil at Fujairah in the UAE as part of India’s strategic petroleum reserve network.

briefs.headline: Economic settlement not resolved: Mallika, Lakshmi
briefs.bodyText:
CHENNAI: Lakshmi Venu and Mallika Srinivasan have said the economic settlement within the Venu Srinivasan (VS) family remains unresolved, disputing suggestions that a division of assets has been completed.
In a joint statement issued amid recent media reports, Lakshmi Venu and Mallika Srinivasan, daughter and wife of Venu Srinivasan, respectively, said no agreement on the division of economic interests had been concluded.
They distinguished this from the broader TVS family partition, agreed upon in 2020 and implemented subsequently, which involved valuation, discussions and mutual consent. They said no comparable process had taken place within their family branch.
According to a statement by Venu Srinivasan, quoted by Republic TV: "The businesses and assets were mine, and I had the full liberty to deal with them as I deemed fit, keeping in mind the best interests of the family members as well as the businesses. I had always believed that the next generation should be given full ownership and control while they are young and have the energy and ideas to build their enterprises. It is with this intent that I carried out a separation between Lakshmi and Sudarshan.
"
His statement also said: "Lakshmi was given to take forward and grow the SCL business, and Sudarshan was given to take forward and grow the motor business. The separation was always about ownership and control.
"The separation was on a fair basis at the time it was done, keeping several factors in mind, including the fact that Mallika Srinivasan, who controls TAFE, had made clear her intention to pass on ownership and control of TAFE to Lakshmi, who is already involved in its management as its vice-chairman. It was carried out openly, transparently, with the knowledge of and after careful consultation with my family."
Lakshmi Venu and Mallika Srinivasan disputed the suggestion that the assets belonged exclusively to one individual who could decide their distribution unilaterally. They also maintained that management roles and arrangements concerning trademarks, brand usage and non-compete obligations should not be treated as substitutes for an economic settlement.
Clarifying TAFE's position, the joint statement by the duo said the company belongs to the Amalgamations Group, a separate family business group in which Mallika Srinivasan is a shareholder, and has no bearing on the economic settlement within the VS family.
"The fundamental issue is not about management positions, which have been compensated appropriately and commensurately. It is about the fair recognition of rightful economic ownership, which remains unresolved," the statement said.

briefs.headline: PERM certifications at 13 IT companies fell to 607 in 9 months from 1,670 in FY25
briefs.bodyText:
BENGALURU: IT firms had shrugged off concerns over their dependence on the US green-card route well before the US administration announced the suspension of PERM processing, with certified applications already declining sharply.
Thirteen major IT services companies recorded 607 certified permanent labour certification (PERM) applications in the first nine months of FY26, compared with 1,670 in FY25 and 1,756 in FY24, according to Kotak Institutional Equities. Kotak has reported certified PERM applications across major IT services companies with Sep fiscal year-ends.
The decline comes as the US administration has suspended new and pending PERM applications involving TCS, Infosys, HCL Technologies, Wipro, Cognizant and Capgemini. PERM is a key labour-certification stage in the process of obtaining employment-based green cards.
TCS recorded just two certifications in the first nine months of FY26, against 505 in FY25 and 597 in FY24. Wipro also had two certifications, compared with 206 in FY25. HCLTech recorded 28, down from 94 in FY25 and six in FY24.
Infosys had 12 certified applications in FY25, while the report shows no figure for the first nine months of FY26 or FY24. 
Cognizant recorded 741 certifications in FY24, but the report does not provide figures for FY25 or the first nine months of FY26. Capgemini had seven certifications in the first nine months of FY26, against 290 in FY25 and 50 in FY24.
Among the other companies covered, LTM recorded 168 certifications in the first nine months of FY26, up from 127 in FY25 and 159 in FY24. Persistent Systems reported 58, compared with 16 in FY25 and 10 in FY24. Mphasis recorded 82 certifications in the first nine months of FY26, against 132 in FY25 and 79 in FY24, while Hexaware Technologies had 73, compared with 24 and one, respectively.

briefs.headline: Rupee gains 96 paise as RBI curbs begin to take effect
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: The rupee rose 96 paise to 95.77 per dollar on Monday after fresh measures to curb dollar demand and speculative positions, even as banks sought relaxation of the new foreign exchange restrictions, more time for compliance and clarity on operational issues. The currency has weakened around 6.5% this year.
The recovery may prove temporary unless underlying pressures ease, economists said. Elevated oil prices, foreign portfolio outflows and a widening trade deficit continue to weigh on the currency. The sustainability of the rupee's recovery will depend on crude oil prices, capital flows, foreign exchange reserves and whether underlying balance-of-payments pressures ease, dealers said. Monday's gain was the highest in over six months. The rupee had gained nearly 124 paise on April 2. Monday's surge was among the top five gains in the last five years as well.
The Foreign Exchange Dealers' Association of India (FEDAI) petitioned RBI seeking relaxation and deferment of the measures. Banks flagged additional client documentation, uncertainty over pricing products to recover compliance costs, and the need for clarity on how frequently reserves must be deposited and reported. 
They also cited the cost of interest on additional reserves parked with RBI, which varies across banks, and the expense of developing customised products to meet the new requirements.
Bond yields, meanwhile, rose as the measures tightened liquidity and raised concerns about further monetary tightening. The 10-year yield climbed to around 7.39%. Banks have also been directed to maintain at least 99% of their required cash reserves with RBI each day during a fortnight, up from 90%, effective Oct 16.

briefs.headline: HCLTech Q2 revenue up 2.2%, narrows FY27 guidance

MUMBAI: HCLTech's dollar revenue rose to $3.7 billion in the Sept quarter, up 2% sequentially and 2.2% year-on-year. In constant currency terms, revenue grew 2.3% sequentially and 2.6% year on year. EBIT margin expanded 131 basis points sequentially and 71 basis points year-on-year to 18.2%.
The company's services business grew 3% sequentially, generating more than $100 million in incremental revenue. About $50 million came from advanced AI and the remaining $50 million from the core business, where HCLTech is gaining market share through AI-driven services.
HCLTech narrowed its FY27 company revenue growth guidance to 2.5%-4% in constant currency terms from the 1%-4% announced in Q1. Services revenue growth guidance was revised to 3%-4% from the earlier range of 1.5%-4.5%. CEO C Vijayakumar said the company retained the midpoint of both guidance ranges despite narrowing them, reflecting caution about extrapolating recent improvements in demand amid a volatile business environment.

briefs.headline: Centre, states to work on widening GST base
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: With GST rate rationalisation and procedural simplification out of the way, the Centre has offered to help the states in widening the base using data analytics, with changes in the return filing system and invoice matching also likely to plug leakages.
"We have had discussions on improving the base and also quality of disclosure... We can leverage technology to increase the base without the exercise being intrusive. We can improve the analytics and work with GST Network (the back-end data arm) on the identified gaps," an official said, adding that some analysis has also been shared with the states. Currently, there are 1.7 crore registered taxpayers and officials indicated that this number can be increased.
They said with changes in returns and the invoice matching system will also help plug revenue leakages, while also making life simpler. Separately, the Centre and the states are looking to encourage e-invoicing, which is likely to be ready by April. Here, there will be an incentive for businesses to move to the new mechanism as govt looks to be "facilitative" instead of mandating things. B2C e-invoicing is also expected to provide data on all entities in the supply chain -- from suppliers to the final seller.
Currently, businesses with average annual turnover of Rs 5 crore have to mandatorily generate e-invoice for B2B sales.
Officials said that most of the changes finalised by the GST Council last week will be implemented from April as some amendments to the laws are required. But the finance ministry is also examining if the move to stop issuing notices for demand under Rs 10,000 can be done through an executive order.
Over the next few weeks officials from the Centre and the states will come together to discuss if there is a need to stop tax credits for the entire chain or only the errant entity should face action. "We will need to undertake analytics and improve coordination between states to get hold of the errant supplier," the official said. At the Council meeting, states sought a review of the proposal . Some of them were of the view that by blocking the credit, they were able to go after some of the players in the chain, which businesses have argued often leads to harassment.
Similarly, some of the states did not allow the plan to allow input tax credit on automobiles to be used by businesses claiming that this will also be claimed when vehicles were put to personal use. The Centre has argued that this may be the case with small businesses or proprietorship firms -- which account for 75% of the credits for vehicle purchases but have only 15% of the amount claimed -- but not with all businesses.

briefs.headline: European car companies will prefer to make in India: Piyush Goyal

Piyush Goyal

"Finally India is going to become the global hub for car manufacturing. Everybody is going to come and manufacture in India and with Europe having such crazy regulations, it is going to be impossible to be competitive. briefs.headline: PC market witnessed a massive contraction in Q3 of 2026: Gartner
briefs.bodyText:
Global personal computer (PC) market witnessed a massive contraction in the third quarter of 2026, with worldwide shipments plummeting 22.4% year-over-year to total 55.4 million units, according to data released by market tracker, Gartner.
This steep downturn has effectively dragged shipment volumes back down to levels last seen in the first quarter of 2023. Unlike previous market slumps driven by excess inventory, this recent collapse was primarily triggered by severe component cost inflation, it said.
“The impact of higher memory and storage costs is now fully reflected in PC pricing. DRAM costs surged five times year-over-year in the second quarter, and PC vendors passed those higher component costs on to customers, driving the steep decline in PC shipments during the third quarter,” said Namrata Banerjee, Principal, Research at Gartner.
PC shipments have fallen to levels last seen in early 2023, though the market dynamics were noticeably different, Mt. Banerjee added.
A fivefold surge in DRAM (Dynamic Random-Access Memory) year-over-year during the second quarter forced PC vendors to pass these higher expenses onto customers, significantly raising average selling prices and making device replacements unaffordable for many buyers.
The crunch spared no major industry players, as all top six worldwide PC vendors reported shipment declines. Market leader Lenovo mirrored the broader industry with a 22.4% year-over-year drop, leveraging its supply chain scale to maintain its top position. HP Inc. suffered the most severe blow among the leading players, recording a sharp 30.9% decline due to its high exposure to price-sensitive consumer and mainstream business segments, according to Gartner.
Meanwhile, tech giant Apple managed to weather the storm better than its peers, registering the lowest shipment decline among the top six vendors and gaining 1.7 percentage points in market share on the back of its mainstream MacBook portfolio.
Overall, scarce component availability forced manufacturers to reprioritise high-priced configurations, prompting corporate clients to limit spending to AI PCs and workstations instead of executing broad-based deployments.

stories.headline: 'We are enough for each other': Shaw, Akriti reunite after calling off engagement
stories.deck: Cricketer Prithvi Shaw and actor-influencer Akriti Agarwal have reconciled weeks after calling off their engagement. Akriti admitted that others’ opinions influenced her decision to separate and said honest conversations helped them reunite. The couple got engaged in March 2026 but parted ways in September. Meanwhile, Shaw is working on his cricket comeback, recently scoring 70 for Maharashtra…
stories.bodyText:
Indian cricketer 
Prithvi Shaw
 and actor-influencer 
Akriti Agarwal
 have decided to give their relationship another chance, weeks after calling off their engagement.
Akriti confirmed their reunion through an Instagram statement on Monday, admitting that other people’s opinions had influenced her decision to end the relationship.
In a post titled "A personal clarification", Akriti said she had allowed people close to her to influence how she viewed Shaw and their relationship.
“When I called off our engagement, I let the opinions of people close to me – who seemed to know our relationship better than we did – influence how I saw my fiancee and our relationship,” she wrote.
“I feel I was misguided, and I made a decision without giving us the honest conversation we deserved.”
Akriti said the two have since had honest conversations, understood each other better and decided to reunite. She also took responsibility for the hurt caused by her earlier decision and asked people to respect their choice.
“Together, we are enough for each other, and we don't need anyone else,” she wrote. Shaw later shared her statement on his Instagram story.
Engagement called off in September
Shaw and Akriti announced their engagement in March 2026, sharing pictures of the proposal on social media.
However, in September, Akriti revealed that they had decided to part ways, citing different goals and circumstances.
Her latest statement confirms that they have reconciled, although neither has publicly explained all the details behind their separation and reunion.
Away from his personal life, Shaw is also working to revive his cricket career.
The 26-year-old rose to prominence after captaining India to the Under-19 World Cup title in 2018 and scoring a century on his Test debut against the West Indies later that year. However, injuries and inconsistent performances have kept him away from the national team.
He moved from Mumbai to Maharashtra ahead of the 2025-26 domestic season in search of a fresh start and scored 222 against Chandigarh in the Ranji Trophy last season.

stories.headline: IPL has helped develop Kiwi players and coaches: NZC chief Geoff Allott
stories.deck: Ahead of India’s tour of New Zealand, NZC CEO Geoff Allott speaks to TOI about hosting the country’s biggest-ever series, record ticket sales, pitches, the IPL’s influence on Kiwi cricket and the enduring bond between the two nations.
stories.bodyText:
What does India’s upcoming tour mean to New Zealand Cricket?
It’s a massive moment. An Indian tour is always one we look forward to, but this will be the biggest tour we’ve ever had in New Zealand. It’s a record for us in terms of the amount of cricket being played in a single series. The quality of the opposition and the respect we have for India make it a mouth-watering contest.
Financially, how significant is a tour by India?
Naturally, there are major commercial benefits, but it’s about a lot more than finances. India are one of the premier teams in world cricket, and whenever they tour New Zealand there’s tremendous excitement among fans, sponsors and broadcasters.
What sort of response have you seen from fans?
It’s been tremendous. In fact, it’s a record for us. We’ve sold more than 85,000 tickets already, and we’re still some time away from the first match. (Oct 22). We’re well above budget and well ahead of where we would normally be. The colour, energy and excitement that come with an Indian tour are something we all enjoy.
Indian fans still remember some of New Zealand’s seam-friendly wickets from the past, especially 2002. What can they expect this time?
We’ve worked really hard over many years to produce high-quality international wickets. Our groundsmen are renowned around the world for the surfaces they prepare. 
We made a conscious decision that you can’t become a top international side unless you’re prepared to play teams on good, even wickets. We want contests between two quality sides.
As the joint-highest wicket-taker at the 1999 World Cup, are you tempted to put the bowling boots back on when you see some of those green pitches?
(Laughs) No, I think those days are behind me. I’ll leave that to the current players. But I understand why people ask the question. The conditions can still offer something for bowlers, especially early in the summer, but our goal is to produce balanced wickets that make for outstanding cricket.
Could we see a dedicated India-New Zealand trophy in the future dedicated to honouring legends of the two countries?
It’s certainly something we’d consider. India and New Zealand have enjoyed a fantastic relationship for a very long time. We compete fiercely on the field, but there is huge respect off it. We’ve had strong historical connections, and it’s a relationship we value enormously.
The IPL has become a major platform for New Zealand players and coaches. How important has it been for New Zealand cricket?
The IPL has been hugely important. It’s a world-leading tournament, incredibly well run by the 
BCCI
. From a New Zealand Cricket perspective, it’s given not only our players but also our coaches tremendous opportunities to grow and develop. Whether it’s exposure to high-performance environments, different coaching styles or working alongside some of the best players in the world, there are enormous benefits.
New Zealand coaches seem to be in demand everywhere. Why do you think that is?
We’ve got plenty of coaches around the world who have done exceedingly well. You look at Stephen Fleming, Brendon McCullum, Daniel Vettori, Jeetan Patel and many others. I think one of the strengths Kiwis bring is the ability to build relationships. Indians and Kiwis connect on a level that goes far beyond cricket. Our coaches adapt well, communicate well and work effectively in different cultures.
Since 2015, New Zealand have reached multiple ICC finals and won the World Test Championship. What’s behind that consistency?
We’re a nation of about five-and-a-half million people, so there’s a saying that we punch above our weight. A lot of it comes down to culture, leadership and the quality of our high-performance system. We have players who are incredibly passionate about representing New Zealand, and that helps us compete with the best teams in the world.
With Kane Williamson, Trent Boult and Tim Southee moving through different stages of their careers, does New Zealand need a superstar figure to sell the game?
No, I don’t think so. Those players are legends and have contributed enormously, but I’m very confident about the talent coming through. The strength of New Zealand cricket has always been its collective culture rather than reliance on one individual.
Has New Zealand’s success in Test cricket increased interest in the format?
We’ve always had a strong affection for Test cricket. The World Test Championship win was obviously a special moment, but Test cricket has deep roots in New Zealand. There’s still something unique about the format. The momentum shifts, the tactical battles and the nuances of the game are incredibly appealing. 
We’re very committed to it.
You have a personal connection with India as well, don’t you?
Yes. I spent 14 years building a food and beverage business in India before taking up this role. It was going to take a lot to drag me away because I love the country and its people. Through cricket and business, I’ve been fortunate to build many relationships in India, and that’s why this series is particularly special for me.
Finally, what are your expectations from the tour?
I think it will be a terrific contest across formats. The rankings show how competitive India and New Zealand are against each other. With record ticket sales, packed venues and two quality teams, we’re expecting a fantastic series and a wonderful celebration of the relationship between our two countries.

stories.headline: Ronaldo on target as Al-Nassr win after security delay
stories.deck: Kick-off was delayed after Saudi Arabia's Civil Defence ​issued a safety warning 15 minutes before the scheduled ⁠start time in Riyadh, which has been targeted by missiles fired from Yemen-based Houthis in recent days.
stories.bodyText:
Cristiano Ronaldo scored Al-Nassr's second goal as the Saudi Pro League champions overcame an hour-long security delay to beat Uzbekistan's Neftchi 3-1 in the AFC Champions League Elite on Monday (October 12, 2026).
Kick-off was delayed after Saudi Arabia's Civil Defence issued a safety warning 15 minutes before the scheduled start time in Riyadh, which has been targeted by missiles fired from Yemen-based Houthis in recent days.
Ange Postecoglou's side shook off the interruption to go in front through Angelo in the 33rd minute with a deflected strike before Ronaldo doubled the lead nine minutes later.
The 41-year-old struck after Sadio Mane delivered a looping cross from the left that Aiman Yahya directed into Ronaldo's path with his chest and the Portuguese forward lashed the ball into the bottom corner with a shot on the turn.
Alisher Odilov pulled one back for Neftchi six minutes into the second half but Ikromjon Alibaev's red card for a foul on Mohamed Simakan in the 65th minute and an own goal by Anvarjon Gofurov 13 minutes later sealed the win for Al-Nassr.
Meanwhile, defending champions Al-Ahli scored twice in the second half to pick up their first win of the new campaign as Marino Pusic's side beat Al-Wasl from the United Arab Emirates 3-1.
Roger Ibanez put Al-Ahli ahead with a 20th minute header but Pedro Malheiro levelled in the third minute of first-half stoppage time.
Goals from Trincao and Feras Al-Brikan in the 58th and 91st minutes respectively moved Al-Ahli onto four points from their opening two matches.
"We created also in the first half but in the second half we made our goals and I think that was the difference," said Trincao. "Physically we were a little bit better and that was the key to changing the game."
Houssine Rahimi scored twice as Al-Ain defeated Air Force Club 4-1 in Basra, while Hossein Goudarzi's 60th minute goal earned Iran's Esteghlal a 2-1 win over Al-Gharafa.
A last minute penalty from Dostonbek Khamdamov salvaged a 1-1 draw for Pakhtakor against Brendan Rodgers' Al-Qadsiah in Tashkent while Tractor from Iran were held to a 0-0 draw by Qatar's Al-Shamal.

stories.headline: My Olympics preparation is not going to change much: Pranavi Urs
stories.deck: The golfer says the experience in Hangzhou helped her in Aichi-Nagoya where she won the individual gold and the team silver; feels that she benefitted by playing on the Ladies European Tour
stories.bodyText:
Lakshman Singh in 1982 (New Delhi). Shiv Kapur in 2002 (Busan). Pranavi Urs in 2026 (Aichi-Nagoya). For only the third time in history, an Indian golfer won the individual gold at the Asian Games but this one was a bit more special - no Indian woman had achieved this before the 23-year-old from Karnataka. The journey to the top step of the podium had its ups and downs but Pranavi stayed strong, patient and eventually finished the job.
In a media interaction facilitated by the Sports Authority of India, Pranavi shares snippets from the dramatic final day in Japan and how a certain Rory McIlroy played a role in her victory, what this gold means for women’s golf in India, and the way forward:
What does being the first Indian woman golfer to win an individual Asian Games gold medal mean to you?
I’ll always be the first. There are going to be multiple winners after me but I’m the one who set that record. For me, that means the world.
What is the next first that you want to chase after this?
Either to win a Major or an Olympic medal.
Can you recap the final hole?
When I hit that tee shot, I knew I hit it well and I was going to cover the water. It’s a difficult hole. When Shannon (Singapore’s Shannon Tan, the bronze medallist) was in the bunker, with that pin position, she wasn’t going to hit it close. And Ruoning (China’s Ruoning Yin, the silver medallist) also couldn’t hit the shot because she had a long iron in. With my distance, I had an advantage. I just had to keep the ball in play after the second shot. And at the time, I also didn’t know I was going to win. I thought making par would force a playoff. Little did I know that the last putt that I hit was a putt to win.
You didn’t know that you were putting for the win?
No, I didn’t. I was, perhaps, too zoned in and I had one of Shannon’s scores wrong on my scorecard because I was marking hers. I thought I needed to putt. Maybe, there’s a playoff and I’ll still have a medal chance. I didn’t know and that’s why I didn’t celebrate after I won. I wish I had known.
If you could go back in time and you knew that the final putt would win you the gold medal, how would you celebrate?
I don’t know because I haven’t really thought about it. I’ve played so many different victory celebrations of mine in my head. I don’t know which one I was going to do. Maybe just a fist bump. It was so surreal that that happened and I didn’t know.
What went wrong when you had a triple bogey early in the final round?
I just got unlucky. It wasn’t even a bad shot. I just started a bit right and ended up in the bunker. Normally, if it’s a plugged ball, you still have a chance but I didn’t really have one. Then, I hit the shot and it came back in my divot, which was deeper. I hit my shot again and it returned to the same spot. So, I was helpless. Now, looking back at it, I wish I had taken an unplayable and things could have maybe played out a bit different but I’ve still got the medal, so I’m not complaining.
How did you mentally bounce back from the triple bogey?
I’ve been working with my psychologist for years now. At the end of the day, the goal is to keep calm when you’re nervous, stick to your game plan, don’t think about anything else and just focus on what you need to do and what’s in your control more than the outcome. On the fourth hole, she (Yin) went one shot ahead and I’m someone who loves chasing. I thought, “You’ve got nothing to lose. You’ve hit rock bottom now. The worst thing has already happened.”I just stayed patient.
Did the experience of Hangzhou help in the final stages in Aichi-Nagoya?
Yes. I knew what to expect this time and how it really works. Being in a team event as well, I knew what I was stepping into whereas in China, it was my first time playing and representing the country. I was not as experienced three years ago. Since China, I’ve secured my card on the LET (Ladies European Tour). I’ve played in a lot of different conditions. I’ve put myself in a lot of different positions. I’ve also put myself in positions where I was in Japan. So, that experience helped me calm my nerves a little bit.
When you said that you were so zoned in that you didn’t know you were about to win, is it a good thing or is it a bad thing to be so locked in?
If I’m getting a gold, then it’s definitely good. Maybe for my social media, it isn’t because I didn’t celebrate. So, I don’t have a lot of pictures of me celebrating. But jokes apart, it’s good as it shows how much you were invested in the game on that particular day, regardless of what happened or under the circumstances I was in. When we were on the 18th green, they called out our names before we could putt, saying we’re so-and-so (positions). I don’t remember that at all.
How significant is this gold when you look at the growth of women’s golf, especially in India?
The greatest joy and pride that I have is to give back to the sport because the sport has given me everything.It’s given more than I could have asked for. If I could win a medal and grow the sport in India, that means the world to me. Not just people in bigger cities but even in villages and smaller towns, if they can see what I did and somehow pick up a club, enjoy the sport or even get to know about the sport, that’s still growth.
You’ve played a lot on the LET tour and a few events on the LPGA as well. Going forward, what do you think you need to do to be a more permanent member on the LPGA tour?
There are certain stats that I need to work on. My coach (Steven Giuliano) and I have been working towards that.And that’s why I feel like my game has also improved so much from the first half of the season. I’m going to continue to do that.
Aditi Ashok’s fourth-place finish at the Tokyo Olympics changed a lot of things for golf in India. Do you feel that you actually winning gold, albeit in a different competition, is a seminal moment in women’s golf in India?
What Aditi did in Tokyo was unreal and that’s when golf in India became popular. I would give all the credits to her. People are comparing me with Aditi and I don’t think I’m as good as her. She’s still way above me and she’s my senior. What she’s done for the sport, I wish and hope to do as much. She’s also a silver medallist at the Asian Games in China.
What kind of decisions were the most important and challenging for you in Japan? Also, how does this gold change your preparation for the Olympics?
The thing that I did on the last hole, if you saw the video, I changed my club on my second shot after I hit the drive. I had a 6-iron but then, I said to my caddy that I’m feeling the adrenaline rush and I can’t be hitting 6-iron because it’s going to go over the green. I’m just going to hit a 7-ironThat was one of the moments where I thought this change might help me get the medal because I didn’t know if it was gold or silver.My preparation for the Olympics is not going to change much. I’m going to be playing a lot of events on the LET. The cutoff date is in June 2028.
How did you celebrate your win?
My parents were there with me. I don’t think it hit all of us that I had won and we didn’t know what was happening. They had a gazillion phone calls and texts so they were overwhelmed as well. And then, the next day we went shopping in Tokyo.
Do you also believe in the power of manifestation?
You can’t just manifest and not do anything. You still have to work hard. Manifestation just shows that that’s your dream and this is what you need to work towards. So, I wouldn’t say you manifest and sit at home doing absolutely nothing.If anything, you work harder because you’ve manifested that and that’s what you want. I do believe in manifestation but that just gives me a goal to work towards.
How was your day prior to the final round?
The night before the final round, me and my psychologist spoke about different scenarios and what start I could have. For the first time, I was more aware of my breath work.Normally, when we have sessions, I’m always goofing around. For the first time, I paid more attention to what she was saying because that’s how nervous I was and that’s how badly I wanted the gold. I had an advantage - a three-shot lead. I had to keep it all together as anything could happen. Till it’s done, it’s not done. While thinking about what I wanted to caption after winning, I was also thinking about things that could go wrong.
On the last hole, of course, you were focusing on yourself but you must have also seen that Yin had a lip out?
I played with her for two days and I don’t think she made a single bogey in those two days and that’s why she’s world number six and former world number one. She’s a Major champion but sometimes, if it’s meant to be, it is, right? Nothing can stop you from winning. I think it’ll just be it.But at the same time, I feel like the way I handled my situation, coming down the stretch, I holed a few important putts, which she went on to miss after me. So, I had to put that pressure on her which I did.
Who is your favourite golfer?
Rory McIlroy. After the third hole, he was one of the people I thought about. It was pretty random. But I thought if he can win the Masters (in 2025) after having a terrible start, so can I (win the gold). That’s one way that got me motivated towards the round as well.
Are you thinking of going to Delhi during the DP World India championship and trying to meet McIlroy and have a moment with him if possible?
Absolutely. My partner (Karandeep Singh Kochhar) is also a golfer. So, he’s playing that event. I’m going to go watch him play anyway. I’ve asked my sources a little bit to get me to meet him (McIlroy). Hopefully that happens. And if that happens, I think I’m going to be more nervous meeting him than winning the gold.

briefs.headline: Sarah, first Zimbabwean female umpire in Women's T20 WC, passes away at 36
briefs.deck: Former Zimbabwe cricketer and umpire Sarah Dambanevana has died in Harare at 36 after months in hospital following a medical procedure. She represented Zimbabwe from 2009 to 2014 before becoming an international umpire. In 2023, she became the first Zimbabwean woman to officiate a World Cup final and later worked at the 2024 and 2025 women's World Cups.
briefs.bodyText:
Former Zimbabwe fast bowler and international umpire Sarah Dambanevana has died in Harare at the age of 36. She passed away on Monday, October 12, after spending months in hospital following a medical procedure in March, Zimbabwe Cricket confirmed.
Dambanevana represented Zimbabwe as a player between 2009 and 2014 before moving into umpiring, where she went on to make history on the international stage.
From player to a trailblazing umpire
Dambanevana began her senior international umpiring career in September 2023. Earlier that year, she became the first Zimbabwean woman to officiate in a World Cup final when she stood in the final of the Under-19 Women's T20 World Cup between India and England in South Africa.
She later officiated at the Women's T20 World Cup in the UAE in 2024, becoming first Zimbabwean female umpire to do so.
She also took field in the Women's ODI World Cup in India and Sri Lanka in 2025. At the latter tournament, she was part of the first all-female panel of match officials.
In total, she officiated in 63 senior international matches, including 42 women's T20 Internationals, 11 women's ODIs and 10 men's T20 Internationals. 
She also worked in domestic cricket and international youth tournaments. Before becoming an umpire, she played for Zimbabwe, including at the 2011 World Cup Qualifier. She joined the ICC's development panel of umpires in 2022.
Zimbabwe Cricket pays tribute
Zimbabwe Cricket chairman Tavengwa Mukuhlani praised Dambanevana for her contribution to the game as both a player and an umpire.
"Sarah served Zimbabwe with distinction, first as a player and then as an umpire whose ability earned her a place on the world stage," Mukuhlani said. "Watching her stand in a World Cup final was a moment of immense pride for our cricket community and our country. She showed young Zimbabwean women that they belong at the highest levels of the game, including in roles where opportunities had long been limited.
"Through her achievements, she opened doors and gave others the confidence to pursue their own ambitions. We will remember her dedication, her professionalism and her willingness to help others grow. Her passing leaves a painful void in our cricket family, but the example she set will continue to inspire those who follow in her footsteps."

briefs.headline: 2036 Olympics hosts: Ahmedabad vs South Korea, Qatar, Munich, South Africa, Türkiye, Hungary
briefs.deck: As Ahmedabad builds its case to host the 2036 Olympics, it faces competition from cities and countries with different advantages. From Munich’s existing venues and Qatar’s event-ready infrastructure to South Korea’s regional model, South Africa’s continental ambition, Istanbul’s Olympic experience and Hungary’s low-construction approach, each offers challenge, and lessons, for India.
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI:
 The International Olympic Committee (IOC) has confirmed seven interested parties for the 2036 Summer Olympics: India, Germany, Qatar, South Korea, South Africa, Türkiye and Hungary. With the process currently at the dialogue stage, the bids will be shortlisted in March 2027, preferred hosts will be identified in December 2028, and the host will be announced in mid-2029.
Germany's candidate is Munich; South Korea's project is associated with Jeonju and Jeonbuk, as well as Seoul; Qatar's is centred on Doha; and South Africa is considering a multi-city or nationwide model. Hungary has designated Budapest as its central venue, while Türkiye is planning to host the 2036 Summer Olympics in Istanbul and India in Ahmedabad.
South Korea
South Korea is no stranger to hosting the Olympics. Seoul hosted the 1988 Summer Olympics, a landmark event in the country's emergence on the international stage. PyeongChang hosted the 2018 Winter Olympics, giving the country experience of hosting both the Summer and Winter Games.
What is South Korea's 2036 project?
Seoul, South Korea has hosted the Olympics before in 1988. (Reuters)
The domestic selection process produced a significant change in direction. The Korean Sport & Olympic Committee selected Jeonbuk (North Jeolla Province), with Jeonju as its focal city, as the country's domestic candidate. 
The wider discussion has also involved Seoul, which has its own infrastructure and Olympic legacy.
Jeonbuk has been pushing an Olympic plan that uses venues across the province and other Korean cities, while Seoul's supporters have argued that its existing facilities and transport infrastructure make it a more credible option.
The regional approach could distribute the benefits of the Games beyond the capital. It also raises a practical question: how will the country present a single, coherent proposal to the IOC when different domestic stakeholders have championed different hosting models?
What should Ahmedabad learn from South Korea?
South Korea's advantage is its proven experience in delivering the Olympics. Ahmedabad, by contrast, is building its case around the 2030 Commonwealth Games and the possibility of using the Olympics to transform India's sporting ecosystem.
The comparison, therefore, is not simply about how many stadiums each city has. It is about whether Ahmedabad can offer the IOC an equally convincing account of how the venues will work, how athletes will move between them, and what will remain after the Games.
Qatar
Qatar showcased its abilities by hosting the 2022 FIFA World Cup. (Reuters)
Qatar is selling accumulated investment and operational readiness. Rather than making the Olympics the starting point for a major infrastructure build-out, it wants to demonstrate that much of the necessary infrastructure is already in place.
Doha previously sought to host the Summer Olympics in 2016 and 2020 but failed to reach the final stage of either selection process. The 2016 project was rejected at the applicant stage, while the 2020 campaign did not make the final group of candidate cities.
Since then, Qatar has substantially expanded its major-event credentials. Its record includes:
- The 2022 FIFA World Cup.
- The 2023 AFC Asian Cup.
- The 2024 World Aquatics Championships.
- The 2030 Asian Games, which Qatar is scheduled to host.
This record gives Qatar something that a first-time Olympic host cannot easily replicate: experience in managing a major-event ecosystem, including stadiums, accommodation, transport, broadcasting and international sporting operations.
What is Qatar's 2036 project?
A view of the Khalifa International Stadium in Qatar. 
Qatar's pitch is centred on Doha and the wider metropolitan area, with Lusail and Al Rayyan among the locations relevant to its existing sports infrastructure.
The Qatar Olympic Committee has said that approximately 95% of the required sports infrastructure is already available. The final project will still need to establish the suitability of venues, their capacity, operating arrangements and any gaps that must be addressed.
Its approach is tied to Qatar National Vision 2030, with an emphasis on sustainability, inclusion, legacy and limiting unnecessary construction. The country is also looking to build on the facilities and experience developed for the 2022 World Cup.
One important complication is the calendar. Doha's summer temperatures could make a conventional July-August Olympics difficult. Qatar's 2022 World Cup was moved to November and December because of the heat, and a Summer Olympics in Qatar would face a comparable question about competition conditions and scheduling.
What should Ahmedabad learn from Qatar?
How the 2036 Olympics host selection process will work. (Image: IOC)
Qatar sets the benchmark for infrastructure readiness and delivery experience. Its challenge is not whether it can build major sports facilities, but whether it can make the case for a Summer Olympics that meets athletes' needs, accounts for the climate and delivers an enduring public legacy.
Ahmedabad can counter with a different argument: hosting would accelerate the development of a sports ecosystem in a country with a vast population and a large potential athlete base. However, the Indian proposal will need to be precise about which facilities already exist, which are planned and how each investment will be used after 2036.
Qatar's experience also offers a warning for India: successfully delivering one mega-event does not, by itself, settle questions about long-term legacy, sustainability or international scrutiny.
Munich, Germany
Munich had hosted the 1972 Summer Olympics. The 2036 Games will mark 100 years since Berlin hosted the controversial 'Nazi Games'. (AP)
Munich, which hosted the 1972 Games, wants to show that a modern Olympics need not be a giant construction project. Its proposition centres on existing venues, short distances, a familiar Olympic setting and the conversion of Games infrastructure into long-term public assets.
The year 2036 has particular significance: it would fall exactly 100 years after the Berlin Games, which the Nazi regime exploited for propaganda. This gives Germany an opportunity to frame the event around democratic values and a very different modern identity, but it also makes the anniversary politically sensitive.
Germany's domestic selection process was competitive. Munich defeated Cologne-Rhine-Ruhr in the German Olympic Sports Confederation's selection, winning by 90 votes to 51. Hamburg's earlier plans had been rejected in a referendum, while Berlin withdrew its proposal. Munich was eventually selected as Germany's candidate for the 2036, 2040 or 2044 Games.
What is Munich's 2036 project?
Munich enjoys the support of its locals in its 2036 Olympics bid. (AP)
The German Olympic Sports Confederation's official concept, Munich for Germany, has several distinguishing features:
- Existing facilities: The Olympic Park, which hosted events in 1972, is the centrepiece.
- Short distances: Munich wants to keep a large proportion of competition venues within a compact geographical area.
- A recognisable city setting: Locations such as the English Garden, Nymphenburg Palace and Odeonsplatz feature in the wider vision.
- Post-Games housing: The Olympic and Paralympic Village is intended to become a climate-neutral, accessible neighbourhood for more than 10,000 people.
- Sustainability: The bid promotes the circular use of resources and a legacy that extends beyond the event itself.
The DOSB says approximately half of all competitions would take place in the Olympic Park. The concept is intended to reduce the need for new construction and make use of Munich's existing sporting infrastructure.
Munich's domestic public mandate is also notable: 66.4% of residents voted in favour of hosting the Olympic and Paralympic Games in a referendum.
What should Ahmedabad learn from Munich?
Munich's strongest argument is that it may not need to build as much as its rivals. That is a direct challenge to Ahmedabad's model. India's plans involve a major programme of urban development and sports infrastructure around the city. Munich, by contrast, is presenting existing venues and legacy reuse as competitive advantages.
For Ahmedabad, the lesson is to explain not just how much infrastructure will be developed, but also how much can be reused, how much it will cost to maintain and what the city will gain in return. A compelling Olympic proposal must be an urban development plan as well as a sports master plan.
South Africa
South Africa had hosted the 2010 FIFA World Cup. (AP)
South Africa wants to bring the Summer Olympics to Africa for the first time. Its case combines the symbolic significance of being the first African host with the country's existing experience of delivering major international sporting events.
South Africa has never hosted an Olympic Games. Its major-event record includes the 1995 Rugby World Cup and the 2010 FIFA World Cup.
The latter is especially relevant because it demonstrated the country's ability to stage a global event across multiple venues and cities. It also offers an example of how a major tournament can be used to develop or upgrade infrastructure.
The country has explored hosting the Olympics for several years, with the government approving its entry into the IOC's Continuous Dialogue process for a potential 2036 or 2040 Games.
What is South Africa's 2036 project?
South Africa are hoping to become the first African nation to host the Olympics. (Getty Images)
The proposal initially outlined by South African Olympic leadership is a multi-city model involving Cape Town, Johannesburg and Durban.
The logic is to distribute venues and responsibilities across existing urban centres rather than force the entire event into one city. It draws inspiration from the use of multiple locations at Paris 2024 and aims to make greater use of existing facilities.
The three cities offer different strengths:
- Cape Town: A globally recognisable setting and a proposed centre of the national project.
- Johannesburg: Major-event experience and established sporting infrastructure, including FNB Stadium.
- Durban: Existing major sports facilities, including Moses Mabhida Stadium.
The final configuration remains subject to development. South African officials have also indicated that a preferred host city would need to be selected as the project progresses.
What should Ahmedabad learn from South Africa?
South Africa and India are both trying to make a larger historical argument through the Olympics. For South Africa, success would mean hosting the first Summer Olympics on African soil. For India, it would mean hosting the country's first Olympic Games and taking a major step towards its ambition of becoming a global sporting power.
Both can argue that hosting would expand participation and create a wider sporting legacy. Both also need to show that their national ambitions are backed by credible funding, reliable governance and realistic plans for coordinating the host locations.
The key distinction is that South Africa's project is explicitly designed to spread the Games across multiple cities. India's proposal is centred on Ahmedabad, even though the benefits of hosting would be national.
Türkiye
Turkiye has made five unsuccessful attempts at winning the bid to host the Olympics. (Getty Images)
Istanbul is trying to turn repeated Olympic disappointment into a stronger, more mature proposal, using existing infrastructure and upcoming international events to demonstrate readiness. Istanbul has made five previous unsuccessful attempts to host the Summer Olympics: 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012 and 2020.
The 2020 campaign is especially relevant because Istanbul reached the final vote, finishing behind Tokyo. The city therefore has experience of an Olympic campaign at the highest level but has yet to convince the IOC to award it the Games.
Türkiye's current bid process has been underway for several years. The Turkish National Olympic Committee (TMOK) says it formally backed Istanbul's candidacy in April 2024 and entered the IOC's Continuous Dialogue process.
What is Türkiye's 2036 project?
Istanbul's proposal combines existing venues and infrastructure with a wider national effort to demonstrate its ability to organise major competitions.
The city's Olympic authorities, the Ministry of Youth and Sports, Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality and the Turkish Paralympic Committee have been involved in presenting the project's vision to the IOC. Their work has addressed the expected impact of the Games, the legacy plan and the relationship between the Olympic project and Istanbul's urban development objectives.
The most important practical milestone is the 2027 European Games, which Türkiye intends to use as a rehearsal for its Olympic ambition.
Tokyo had edged Turkiye in winning the bid to host the 2020 Games. (Getty Images)
TMOK has described the event as a live rehearsal and a test of confidence. The intention is to demonstrate venue readiness, transport and logistics, operational capacity and the ability to work with international sporting bodies before the IOC makes its decision on the 2036 Games.
Türkiye's government has also pointed to its experience of hosting major sporting competitions, ongoing investment in swimming facilities and the availability of an Olympic Village. Those claims will need to be assessed alongside the complete competition-venue plan and the wider logistics of the proposed Games.
What should Ahmedabad learn from Türkiye?
Istanbul's advantage is that it has repeatedly pursued the Olympics and understands the demands of the bidding process. However, its history also demonstrates that persistence and a strong city identity do not guarantee success.
The 2027 European Games offer a useful parallel with Ahmedabad's role in the 2030 Commonwealth Games. Both cities have a major multisport event that can serve as evidence of their ability to host something larger.
For Ahmedabad, the critical question will be whether the Commonwealth Games become a genuine test of operational readiness and long-term planning, rather than simply a milestone on the way to an Olympic bid.
Hungary
Hungary had initially bid to host the 2024 Olympics but it was later withdrawn. (AP)
Hungary is exploring a bid to host the 2036 Olympic and Paralympic Games in Budapest, with a vision centred on existing and temporary venues rather than the construction of new permanent stadiums. The proposed model envisages at least 80% of events taking place in Hungary, with the possibility of sharing venues with neighbouring countries.
Budapest has pursued Olympic hosting ambitions for the 1916, 1920, 1936 and 1960 Games, but none resulted in the city being awarded the event. Its most recent campaign was for the 2024 Olympics, but it was withdrawn in February 2017 after the Momentum Movement gathered approximately 266,000 signatures demanding a referendum on the proposal.
Since then, Hungary has hosted several major international sporting events, including the 2017 and 2022 World Aquatics Championships and the 2023 World Athletics Championships. These events have strengthened the country's experience in organising international competitions, although an Olympic bid would still require broad political consensus and firm financial guarantees.
What is Hungary's 2036 project?
The proposed Games would draw on Hungary's existing sporting infrastructure, including Puskás Aréna, the National Athletics Centre, MVM Dome and Duna Aréna. Where suitable facilities are unavailable, organisers could consider temporary venues or explore sharing facilities with other countries. Preliminary discussions have included possible venues in Vienna, Bratislava, Košice, Brno, Ljubljana, Zagreb, Belgrade and Cluj-Napoca, although no final agreements have been reached.
What should Ahmedabad learn from Hungary?
Budapest has pursued Olympic hosting ambitions for the 1916, 1920, 1936 and 1960 Games. (Getty Images)
Hungary's proposition is about hosting the Olympics with less new permanent construction, while Ahmedabad's is about using the Olympics to accelerate sporting and urban development.
- Venues: Hungary prioritises existing and temporary facilities, potentially supplemented by venues across Central Europe. Ahmedabad's plans centre on a proposed sports enclave and wider infrastructure development.
- Legacy: Hungary emphasises avoiding underused stadiums and investing in infrastructure that Budapest already needs. Ahmedabad frames the Games as a catalyst for wider participation and India's sporting ambitions.
- Experience: Hungary has recently staged major international championships. Ahmedabad's 2030 Commonwealth Games offer an opportunity to demonstrate its ability to deliver a multisport event.
- Main obstacle: Hungary needs political agreement and a workable cross-border model. Ahmedabad needs to demonstrate that its infrastructure plans, funding, governance and operational capabilities can meet Olympic requirements.
- The key contrast: Hungary asks whether the Olympics can be staged with minimal new permanent stadium construction. Ahmedabad asks whether the Olympics can justify and accelerate a major programme of development.
What is Ahmedabad's plan for the 2036 Games?
Ahmedabad will host the 2030 Commonwealth Games. (PTI)
India's campaign is framed around the vision "Rising Together" and the idea that hosting the Games could transform the country's sporting ecosystem, rather than merely stage a fortnight of competition. The Indian Olympic Association (IOA) has described the ambition as an opportunity to increase participation, strengthen communities and create opportunities through sport.
IOA CEO Raghuram Iyer has also made the ambition explicit: India wants to become a sporting superpower, with the longer-term goal of entering the world's top five or top 10 sporting nations.
India's own project
- Sports City: Plans associated with the Commonwealth Games include 11 sports complexes and complementary facilities such as gyms, swimming pools and training spaces.
- Municipal investment: Ahmedabad's draft municipal budget for 2026-27 earmarked ₹17,018 crore for development, including mobility, sustainability and urban development.
- 2030 Commonwealth Games: These provide a nearer-term opportunity to test venue delivery and event operations.
- 2038 Asian Games: India has also pursued Ahmedabad as a possible host, potentially creating a sequence of major multisport events leading towards the Olympic ambition.

briefs.headline: Pope withdraws from Afghan league draft amid concerns over treatment of women
briefs.deck: England batter Ollie Pope has withdrawn from the Afghanistan Premier League draft amid concerns over the Taliban’s treatment of women and girls. England cricket director Rob Key said participation was a personal moral decision, despite the ECB’s refusal to arrange bilateral series with Afghanistan. Former England batter Dawid Malan remains in the draft, highlighting the conflict between ethical…
briefs.bodyText:
England batter 
Ollie Pope
 has withdrawn from the draft for the inaugural Afghanistan Premier League (APL), which is scheduled to take place in the United Arab Emirates later this year. His decision comes amid debate over whether English cricketers should participate in the competition because of the Taliban’s treatment of women and girls in Afghanistan.
Pope was expected to be the only centrally contracted England player in the draft. However, his withdrawal was understood to be his own decision, rather than a direct result of discussions with England director of cricket Rob Key. Players need a No Objection Certificate (NOC) from the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) to participate in overseas leagues.
“Legally it is hard to stop players going over and playing in these competitions,” Key told the Test Match Special podcast, as quoted by BBC. “It becomes a moral judgement and players have to be prepared to take the right moral stance.
“Personally, and it is easy for me to say, I would not go and play. But it is down to the player to make that decision.”
The debate over cricket and human rights
The ECB has refused to arrange bilateral series against Afghanistan since the Taliban returned to power in 2021. However, England continue to face Afghanistan in major international tournaments, including the World Cup and Champions Trophy.
Key also expressed his opposition to the treatment of women in Afghanistan. “I don't agree with the way women have been treated in Afghanistan,” said Key. “The way things happen out there is not something I agree with so it is not something I would go and do.”
Former England batter Dawid Malan, however, is among those entered in the APL draft, alongside Moeen Ali, James Vince and James Rew. Malan said players faced a difficult choice between personal beliefs and earning a living.
“As a player it is tough because you have what is morally right and what is by the law,” Malan said, adding that players often needed their cricket boards to take a clear position.
He also questioned why players were expected to make individual decisions when England continued to play Afghanistan in global tournaments.

briefs.headline: Abhishek switches off before turning on the style
briefs.deck: Abhishek’s assault was so good that the Men in Maroon immediately switched to damage-limitation mode: he raced to his 14th T20I half-century off just 18 deliveries
briefs.bodyText:
As Abhishek Sharma readied himself to tackle the press, one could not help but admire the glitter of his jewellery.
But even that did not come close to the spark which radiated off his effervescent strokeplay in the 14-run victory over the West Indies in the third T20I here on Sunday. For a change, the India opener opted to begin his eventful ride on first gear rather than going full throttle from ball one.
Abhishek, mindful that Roston Chase had had his number in the previous two duels, played the ball along the ground against the off-spinner and speedster Shamar Joseph in the opening part of the PowerPlay. The calm was followed by a storm, whose impact Windies could not survive until the 10th over.
The 26-year-old, known for treating bowlers with disdain, had to “respect” Chase and play a waiting game in order to be successful in the match.
“It (hitting mostly on the off-side) was not a deliberate plan. But I knew that they had a plan for me, so I had to play better than that. With the off-spinner bowling the first over, it was a battle between him and me. I gave him respect in the first over because he has been bowling really well in this series. My plan went really well,” Abhishek reflected on his approach during the 69-run knock.
For the marauding southpaw, opposition-specific pre-series training and “uncomfortable” sessions have been vital to stay on top of his game. “Preparation is really important if I want to continue playing like this and utilise the PowerPlay. It depends on the team and the bowlers I am going to face,” Abhishek said.
“I want to execute my plan really well and dominate as well. As an attacking batter, I have to be ready for all plans when facing world-class bowlers. I make myself uncomfortable in practice so that I am not surprised in a match,” he added.
Abhishek’s assault was so good that the Men in Maroon immediately switched to damage-limitation mode: he raced to his 14th T20I half-century off just 18 deliveries.
“He is a world-class player... kudos to him. We tried to be as defensive as possible and make him get singles and doubles rather than boundaries. It was a matter of trying to pull him back,” Shamar Springer admitted after being at the receiving end.
After all, for India, Abhishek is the gift that keeps on giving.

briefs.headline: Bowlers — a fraternity that has been on a hiding
briefs.deck: There is much to be said of the advantages of chasing in India at this time of the year, when the dew is quite pronounced and gripping the ball in the second half of a match, especially for the spinners, is practically impossible
briefs.bodyText:
Not till the sixth outing in a cluster of eight did a team batting first finally manage to successfully defend a total. India’s 14-run victory in Sunday’s third Twenty20 International had to be earned the hard way, but at least it provided some solace to a fraternity that has been on a hiding to nothing since West Indies’ snappy white-ball tour of India began in Thiruvananthapuram on September 27.
There is much to be said of the advantages of chasing in India at this time of the year, when the dew is quite pronounced and gripping the ball in the second half of a match, especially for the spinners, is practically impossible. It’s not as if bowlers don’t account, or prepare, for this scenario. At practice, they often use wet, slippery balls to try and replicate the conditions they will most likely be confronted with in a match situation, but the nets does not entail the same pressure to deliver as a match, and therefore no amount of training can translate to perfecting a most difficult craft.
It is certainly no coincidence that the Indore victory came when there was no dew, thereby facilitating a hint of reverse swing expertly utilised by Arshdeep Singh, India’s highest wicket-taker in T20Is. Of course, India were also well served by the likes of Prince Yadav and Nitish Kumar, who delivered pinpoint yorkers at the death with great regularity. But even here, their cause was helped by a dry ball which they could send down with control, unlike a slippery orb that doesn’t quite leave the hand as the bowler would like it to be.
Veritable run-fest
The One-Day International series provided a veritable run-fest, with Thiruvananthapuram somewhat of an outlier even though the Caribbeans got off to a frenetic start. John Campbell and centurion Justin Greaves added 135 for the opening wicket in just 114 deliveries to raise visions of a mammoth target on a pancake pitch until Kuldeep Yadav spun a wicked web in the middle overs with his tantalising left-arm wrist-spin. Again, Kuldeep operated in natural light with dew still to make an appearance; his craft shone through as he finished with four for 40 to ensure West Indies didn’t post more than 295, a total reined in with a whopping 50 deliveries to spare as Shubman Gill and Virat Kohli tore into the bowling.
Run-making touched ridiculous proportions three nights later in Guwahati. And yes, ridiculous is being used advisedly.
Campbell, red-hot skipper Shai Hope and the impressive Amir Jangoo provided the first instance of three batters slamming hundreds in the same ODI innings, propelling West Indies to 405 for seven. That’s more than eight runs an over for 50 overs, an extraordinary accomplishment that would guarantee victory 999 times out of 1,000. Only once before, a decade back, had a larger score been hunted down (by South Africa against Australia) internationally, so West Indies would have entertained some designs of squaring the series, but only some designs because they knew that even a run-rate of 8.10 didn’t hold any guarantee.
Their worst fears came true as the prayers of the Guwahati crowd were comprehensively answered. As facetious as it might sound, there was an unmistakable inevitability to India’s march to victory, this time attained also by eight wickets with 39 deliveries to spare. At the forefront again was Gill, who joined his predecessor Rohit Sharma as the only batter to smack more than one ODI double-ton. Gill’s partner-in-crime in the decimation of the bowling was Rohit; their opening salvo of 255, in 158 deliveries – is this even real?! – made this singularly one-way traffic. Evidently, no score is safe anymore. India mounted their highest successful run-chase but they did so without breaking sweat. It was great for the fans, who soaked in a very popular home victory, but what about the bowling fraternity? What about them indeed?
More carnage was to follow in New Chandigarh in the final, dead-rubber ODI, though this time, the boot was on the other foot. Hope’s grin on calling right lit up an already bright Saturday afternoon, a grin that would have made a Cheshire cat weak with envy when Jayden Seales packed off Gill and Kohli in the third over to leave the hosts gasping at four for two. To get to 351 from that point was a terrific accomplishment, aided by the fact that the early bounce and lateral movement dissipated under the unforgiving sin.
West Indies had never scored that many to win a match, and at various stages, it seemed as if they wouldn’t again, but their skipper didn’t buy into that theory. Having kept wickets for 50 wickets and picked up a groin twitch along the way, he made the most of a fortuitous promotion as opener – where he has tasted unparalleled ODI success – with an innings for the ages. Hobbling and wincing, he found a second wind to batter India into submission, raising victory with ten deliveries to spare.
Two National record chases in four nights set it up beautifully – for everyone except the bowlers – heading into the five-match T20I series. Once again, the start was flattering; West Indies floundered against Indian spin in high-scoring Lucknow, shot out for 171 with Axar Patel, Kuldeep and debutant Naman Dhir taking seven wickets between them. It was a total India would have reeled in in their sleep; with skipper Shreyas Iyer choosing that night to bring up his maiden century, it was all over in the blink of an eye, with 32 deliveries in reserve. Were we in store for a more equitable contest between bat and ball?
No sir, we certainly were not.
Over to Ranchi, and game two. Sanju Samson, that infuriatingly inconsistent opener who oscillates between the dreamy and the nightmarish with frustrating frequency, shed a lean trot with a blazing 82, and the captain and his deputy, Tilak Varma, produced an exhilarating final kick to propel India to 249 for five. It was worth more than West Indies’ 405 in the second ODI in all ways imaginable, yet it proved remarkably inadequate. Remarkably.
India plucked out Kamil Pooran – no relation to the more celebrated Nicholas – and Shimron Hetmyer off successive deliveries through the express Mayank Yadav in the very first over, and when Mayank also cleaned up Rovman Powell, West Indies were up against it at 58 for three. Hope – who else? – and Sherfane Rutherford pushed back spectacularly. There was no time to rebuild, no point in steadying the rocking boat. They both teed off, the left-handed Rutherford and his right-handed captain matching each other blow for pulverising blow while adding 120. Rutherford missed out on a century but Hope wasn’t to be denied, powering his team past the finish line with Romario Shepherd for company. It was the second time in three matches (and two different formats) that West Indies had completed a record chase. That they reached 252 with nine deliveries to spare amply demonstrated the dominance of the bat over the ball, which is why India’s 14-run win in Indore assumes greater significance even though they had an impressive 223 to defend.
At the interval, the pundits were busy dissecting if 223 was enough. Imagine that. More than 11 runs an over, and the experts are debating if the team batting first was a few short. Where are we headed? Is this how it is going to be, with towering edifices erected in the evening and razed to the ground by night? Will game after game follow a monotonous pattern of ball-bashing, aided by flat decks, small boundaries, light bats with extended sweet spots, and a profusion of power and cheekiness that leave bowlers tearing their hair out in frustration?
Both after winning in Guwahati and losing in Ranchi, India head coach Gautam Gambhir called for a greater balance between bat and ball. He lamented the punishment the bowlers (from both sides) were being subjected to. He did acknowledge that India should have done better in Ranchi when they had nearly 250 on the board, and you couldn’t argue with that because in some ways, as harsh as it might sound, the bowlers have readymade excuses and therefore carry the belief that they can be excused any mauling.
It’s against this backdrop that one recalls Josh Hazlewood’s remarks during IPL 2026, when he held forth on the challenges of bowling in T20 games, especially in the first six overs when only two boundary-riders are allowed.
“I think it’s definitely nice for the crowds to watch balls flying into the stands,” the Australian quick, one of the heroes of Royal Challengers Bengaluru’s back-to-back IPL triumphs, observed in April. “From a bowler’s point of view, it almost takes the pressure off a little bit because the batsmen are expected to get off to good starts. They’re expected to score big runs, they’re expected to get 230 runs probably every T20 innings they play.”
The Aussie great then held forth on the virtues of defensive bowling, reiterating that especially in 20-over cricket, it is not always imperative to go looking for wickets every ball. “If you can get a batter on two off six balls, the pressure that they’re under in that situation is huge,” he pointed out. “You can just see a player almost melt out there in the middle, they just cannot find the gap, cannot find the boundary. I feel like that’s the biggest pressure in the game now, it almost releases the pressure (on the bowlers) a little bit.”
That’s something Gambhir alluded to in Ranchi, and Nitish harped on after the Indore victory.
While it is true that the best dot ball is the one that comes with a ‘W’ attached to it, when the dice is loaded in favour of the batter and the odds are stacked against the bowler, it is essential to bowl within oneself and do the unglamorous rather than embrace bluster and bravado. Defensive bowling is a fine art – ask a Fanie de Villiers, or a Gavin Larsen or Chris Harris – and doesn’t mean that one doesn’t have the requisite skills to take wickets. It’s just an honest and intelligent acknowledgement of how things stand instead of giving in to ego and trying to show who the boss is.
White-ball bowling hasn’t quite evolved as dramatically and with as much impact as batting, which is understandable because cricket is, after all, a batter’s game.
But unless these ‘my batting strongest’ battles are more evenly spaced out, we are in real danger of killing the goose laying the golden eggs.
