briefs.headline: Marathas outlast Archers in an exciting shootoff
briefs.bodyText:
Mighty Marathas rallied to beat Chero Archers in a thrilling contest of the Archery Premier League season 2 at People’s Plaza on Monday.
Archers, in trademark fashion, started strongly and took the first set. But there was little to separate the teams in the second and third, and the points were split. The final set was also a high-scoring affair and it needed a double check of where the arrows landed before Marathas levelled the scores and took the proceedings into a hit-or-miss shootoff.
Aman Saini and Dhiraj Bommadevara nailed their arrows into the yellow ring.
Mathias Fullerton was the only one to do the same for Archers, giving Marathas a 2-1 win via the tiebreaker.
Later, the Chola Chiefs struggled from the beginning. It was such a woeful display that it couldn’t even get the last arrow out in time and could fare only marginally better in the second set.
Chiefs substituted in Deepika Kumari and Marcus D’Almeida for the third set, but the damage could not repaired. Though the two stepped up, Mete Gazoz nailed a 10 with his final arrow to hand defending champion Rajputana Royals a comfortable win.
Prithviraj Yoddhas’ bid to climb to the top of the table was spoiled by Kakatiya Knights.
Nico Wiener, back in the team, was on song as Knights raced to a 4-0 lead. Nico, Neeraj Chauhan and Elia Canales did enough in the final set to seal the contest despite Jyothi Surekha having a rare off-day.
The scores: Mighty Marathas 4 drew with Chero Archers 4 (74-76, 76-76, 77-77, 77-76). Marathas won 2-1 via tiebreaker.

briefs.headline: Dhir and the art of bouncing back
briefs.bodyText:
If you want to learn the art of instantly bouncing back in an international cricket contest, dial Naman Dhir.
Conceding sixes in an unforgiving format for the bowlers may put many off but not Dhir. Whether you believe it or not, each of the 26-year-old’s first five wickets in T20Is have come immediately after maximums.
While it occurred thrice in the opening India-West Indies match in Lucknow, history repeated itself in the third game in Indore on Sunday, when the off-spinning all-rounder sent back Shimron Hetmyer and Kamil Pooran.
Dhir has not been afraid to tease batters, but he revealed that his primary duty was to deliver tight spells. “My responsibility is to bowl two or three economical overs. In T20 cricket, an attacking option can also be a defensive option because there is nothing better than taking a wicket,” he told JioStar.
Better understanding
“Being a batter helps me understand the [rival] batter’s stance, backlift, guard and the shots he can play. I do not have many variations, so I have to rely on my line and length and vary my pace,” Dhir added.
His wicket-taking ability has allowed India to go with four frontline bowlers.
“I have been seeing him since his u-14 days. The way he is bowling, he is going to do well for India in the next years as well,” Abhishek Sharma was all praise for his India and Punjab teammate.
Dhir would not mind being hit for a six as long as it brings a wicket the very next ball.

briefs.headline: Former pacer Ashis recalls battles against touring Aussies
briefs.bodyText:
Ashis Sinha isn’t too pleased to see the Kerala bowlers toiling on the lifeless wicket against Jharkhand at the Keenan Stadium. He says, “I have never seen a wicket as flat as this one.”
His empathy is understandable. He was a seamer who played for Bihar — Jharkhand would be carved out of the State several years later — as well as East Zone. And he also played football for Bihar in the Santosh Trophy; he was a defender.
Injury may have cut short his career as a cricketer, but not before he could pick up the wickets of former Australian captain Kim Hughes and opener Graham Yallop. Ashis has also scalped a couple of West Indies Test players, as well.
He had played those matches for East Zone. Those days, Test sides used to play several First Class games during tours. Cricketers used to get breathing space between international fixtures.
Ashis has fond memories of removing Hughes and Yallop. “It was my swing that got Hughes lbw and Yallop bowled,” he recalls. “I was clean bowled by Rodney Hogg, who shared the new ball with Geoff Lawson. We won that match at Cuttack in 1979, by four wickets.”
That Australian team also had Allan Border, who had only made his Test debut less than a year ago. “He looked very good even then,” says Ashis. “I also had the opportunity to play against great West Indians like Malcolm Marshall and Alvin Kallicharan on this ground.”
Marshall, in fact, took 11 wickets in that match. “It was indeed a privilege watching him bowl,” says Ashis, who has also been a coach and selector. He was part of the selection committee when India won its maiden under-19 World.
